CANADIAN NATIONAL (WEST INDIES) STEAMSHIPS LIMITED STATEMENT TO CLARIFY POSITION OF COMPANY
speechtext:
I desire to make a statement on the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships.
It has been drawn to my attention that what I had to say on the subject of the future of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited, when the report of that company was being considered by the railways and shipping committee, has created the impression in some quarters that the government has in mind the winding up of the affairs of that company. Such a misconception of the government's intentions may well prejudice the efforts of the steamship company when soliciting business, and I think therefore that the facts should be restated.
What I said before the committee was that while the financial year of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships in 1953 was a disappointing one, the expenses incurred were abnormal owing to abnormal circumstances. I endeavoured to make it clear therefore that 1953 was not a year to look at to obtain a true picture of the situation with respect to the usefulness of the steamships.
The situation is therefore that there is reason to entertain hope that the position of the steamship company will improve, and it is not the intention of the government to abandon this service now. However, the management and the government will keep a very careful eye upon the operations this year in particular in order that we may obtain a true measurement of the usefulness of the service with respect to the future. Consequently those who are interested in the continuation of the service will have an opportunity to demonstrate their willingness to provide sufficient traffic to support it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 6, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it very hard to deal with this budget. It does not itself seem to deal with anything in particular. We have a lot of optimistic hopes by the minister. On the one hand he says, if such and such a thing happens, then the prospect is satisfactory; if it does not happen, things will not be so good; but his conclusion is that the favourable things will happen. This is all very well and fine but the minister gives next to nothing to support his optimistic conclusions.
Next we have a microscopic tax reduction which seems related to nothing in the world except perhaps the minister's desire to leave a good farewell impression in the minds of the children and the users of curling tongs.
The budget reminds me of a book by the late Hilaire Belloc which he entitled "On Nothing".
As I said the other evening, the minister spent an hour and twenty minutes trying to persuade us that the budget was not a budget of blank negation. But I doubt if he even deceived himself. At any rate the immediate and universal feeling throughout the country, so far as one can judge from the press, is that the budget has been a dud.
Let me set on the points on which it is negative. It has nothing for employment, nothing real to relieve the taxpayer, nothing to break the deadlock in wheat, nothing to
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell indicate any intention of improving the efficiency of government, nothing to reassure us that we are not going to have another spate of inflation.
We have come to regard the budget as a statement of what the government has been able to do for the welfare of the Canadian people and its citizens, and second, as a kind of statement of economic conditions in the country.
Judged by this first test, what has the present budget done? The minister will bring in some resolutions, and they will be finally embodied in legislation, but no one can suggest that they will have the slightest effect on the life of the community. They will cause scarcely a ripple. I understand that Birks have announced a 10 per cent reduction on wedding rings. It is not of personal interest to me, but I doubt whether even in these days it will either stimulate or retard the number of marriages that will take place, and I so far have been able to see no other effect of any kind.
I wonder whether it has ever occurred to the minister that if he had only left last year, basking in the sunshine of reduced taxes it would have been a happier thing than in the twilight of today. Gone are the surpluses which rejoiced the heart of the minister, and indeed there is an ugly fear that even the picayune surplus of $4 million which he predicts may not materialize. There is an ugly fear that perhaps he has been a bit optimistic in predicting that, and that he has found it easy to run away from some of the awkward facts. For example, the minister did not find it in his heart to tell us of the large number of industries in which, according to recent reports, production is down: Metal mining, coal mining, non-metal mining, manufacturing as a whole, non-durable manufactures, dairy products, wheat flour, rubber products, tanneries, textiles, clothing, coke and gas products, durable manufacturers as a whole, wopd products, iron and steel products, including primary iron and steel, non-ferrous metal products, non-metallic products and electric power.

The minister's optimism naturally has attracted a good deal of attention, and the Free Press-1 mean the Winnipeg Free Press-has this to say-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I quote:
He makes the surprisingly buoyant assumption that the upturn in the second half of the year will more than compensate for the declines which have been evident in certain branches of industry since the beginning of the calendar year.
The minister makes it clear that he is basing this optimism on his expectation of an upturn in the United States. My only comment on that is that I think it needs a lot more than an upturn in the United States to cure our situation. I think it needs a good deal of effort on our own part. I think it means bringing down our costs in the export trade where we are being hampered at the moment by competition we cannot meet.
Nevertheless, the minister's optimism is attractive. As I listened to it, my mind carried back to a cult-I suppose it was a cult- which was popular a good many years ago, called Coueism. It was a kind of autosuggestion. People muttered incantations to themselves and by that means I suppose they bucked up their morale and the morale of others, and made themselves feel better. One of the incantations I remember was, "Every day and in every way, I am becoming better and better." I suppose the minister has perhaps adopted a little of that and says, "Every day and in every way things are becoming better and better."
I would be the last to deprecate optimism, but I do feel that, while our long-term prospect is brilliant, we should not assume that it is free from perhaps a little of what the minister calls hesitation. I thought that was a nice word. I propose to refer to it later- occasional hesitation. But while I love optimism, I do not think that we should


confuse optimism with wishful thinking. I think what we need is informed and well-based optimism, and I wonder a little whether the minister, humanly enough, just made up his mind that he was going to go optimistic. After all, after seven prosperous years it is hard to contemplate a change and, as I said the other night, I realize that when governments are carried along on the crest of a boom they come to believe that really nothing can go wrong when they are in power-at any rate, that nothing can go seriously wrong. I think they come to believe that they are the darlings of fortune and that fortune will never desert them. So the only world dreamt of in their philosophy is a world where things are always bigger, better and brighter.
Although the minister does admit that there are considerations which give some cause for hesitation, nevertheless he comes definitely down on the side of optimism, but what I would rather call wishful thinking. In this connection it is very interesting to read a short comment on the minister's speech from the Financial Times of London. It is a matter of some interest that the Canadian Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the British Chancellor of the Exchequer presented their budgets on the same day. It did invite comment, and I propose to read a short comment from the Financial Times. The Times says it is obvious from the Canadian budget that finance minister Abbott has based his entire economic policy on an early recovery in the United States. Again, they say:
That, it is worth noting, is more than Mr. Butler, chancellor of the British exchequer ... is willing to do.
Again:
This contrast perhaps also serves to explain why Mr. Abbott had not shown more concern about the marked deterioration in the Canadian trade balance in the past year.
And further:
Evidently it would be very hard indeed for Mr. Abbott to contemplate any other assumption than an early revival of American economic activity without some fundamental changes in his whole financial policy. But that does not make his present policy any less of a calculated risk.
The comment I wish to make on that is that I fail to find very much calculation in the Minister of Finance's assumption of risk. I fear, indeed, that there was not much calculation but that the assumption was a bad assumption, and perhaps even a misleading one. At any rate, there was not enough to support it.
I wish to come now to the definite topics that I want to consider. I wish first to refer

to the continued rise in non-defence expenditure which faces us this year, as in other years, and which we find perplexing and to which there seems to be no answer that the government has been able to find. This year, with things uncertain, we might have expected some kind of retrenchment, but apparently there is none whatever. Private individuals, private corporations, even government corporations like the Canadian National, have to economize. They have to cut their suit according to the cloth. They have to be realistic. But apparently as long as the government has the pocket of the taxpayer open to it it does not become realistic. If only there were a higher power to say to the government, "This is all you have to spend, you cannot spend any more", I think magical things would come about in the way of reorganization.
That has happened in the United States. We are told that they have cut off $7 billion and hope in the coming year to add $5 billion to that. They are taking it seriously. Realism has overtaken them. I suppose one thing which has prevented our taking the situation realistically is that we have had these surpluses. In the United States they have not been misled by surpluses. They have not taken extra money from their people and they have not had these surpluses which are apt to lead a government astray, and I think have led our government astray.
In some mysterious way our government seems to believe there is a divine dispensation which relieves us of the necessity of doing what other people have to do. We apparently do not have to practise prudence and economy. Optimism is the substitute. Of course we all know that that does not make sense. We all know that taxes enter into the cost of production, and we all know that non-defence expenditure should be coming down.
I want to deal with this matter at some length. Let us have a look at our non-defence expenditures since 1948. In the fiscal year ended March, 1948, they were $1,994 million, in round figures. At the end of the next fiscal year they were $1,907 million, a blessed drop to encourage us, but there has been no such encouragement since. At the end of the last fiscal year they were, when you add the old age security fund, $2,697 million, and the present budget provides for $2,892 million. When you take into account the supplement-aries and our non-civil defence expenditures they will be approximately $3 billion this year.
What about our civil service payroll? Permanent and temporary employees increased from 118,000 in 1948 to 135,000 in December, 1953, and the payroll rose from $226 million
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell to $360 million. If we add casuals, ships' crews and so forth, the number of civil servants as of the year 1953 is not 135,000 but 171,000, and the payroll, on the basis of adding casuals, is not $360 million but approximately $475 million. Commenting on this, the Financial Post says:
The trouble with a government job or project is that it never seems to end. Hardly a week passes but some new board or commission is set up, an office opened and a staff hired. But seldom indeed are these groups disbanded even when their original mission has been accomplished. The usual practice is to absorb the staff into some other branches of the service. Over the years that sort of thing adds thousands to the government pay roll but little indeed to government efficiency.
I do not propose to dwell on these figures. I do propose later to dwell as emphatically as I can on what I believe is the need for a close scrutiny into government operations. However, at a time when questions are being asked in the house as to why the C.N.R. has had to reduce its staff, at a time when, from all across Canada, labour departments report unemployment, at a time when there is the greatest anxiety in labour circles about the existing situation, at a time when the unemployed are being asked to tighten their belts and hope for the best and believe the minister has some heaven-sent inspiration when he predicts that all will be well or nearly well in the autumn, at this time the one organization which does not practise what it preaches is the government.
In spite of all this the minister forecasts a surplus. It is microscopic compared to the surpluses of his big days, and even here one wonders whether by the desire to make things look good, by the inability even to contemplate a deficit, he has not been led away by unwarranted optimism. Last year he underestimated the gross national product by $345 million. Nevertheless, even with this windfall of more than a third of a billion dollars, he was high in his revenue estimate by nearly $100 million. If, as some think, the gross national product may be actually lower than last year, if our economic growth has really slowed to a walk, then it could be the minister would have a substantial deficit. I should like to ask him when he replies to state his present estimate of the gross national product.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am sorry if I have forced you to correct me again. As a matter of fact, I was a little bit uneasy. The temptation, of course, to take quotations is extremely strong because free writers so often express your views better than you yourself are able to do so. However, I think I am in the happy position that I have now read all my quotations and that there is no need for me to trespass upon your patience any more.
We in our party have constantly sought to keep before the people of Canada the urgent need for the federal government's reaching agreement with the provincial governments with regard to the reallocation of taxing power. We have done this so often and in such detail, I do not think that I shall repeat this argument today. We have strongly criticized and continue to criticize the obstinate procrastination and ineptitude of the government in not pursuing this matter as they have been urged to do. In the amendment that I propose to move today I shall include the exact words of a paragraph which my leader moved in this house dealing with this subject on November 24, 1952: I regret that the government shows no intention of dealing with a matter which threatens the very foundations of our national unity.
Mr. Speaker, I am coming back to this question of spending because I believe it to be of the very greatest importance. I have not spent a lot of time talking about this or that extravagance because I have come to the conclusion that unless the government is ready to do what it as yet has utterly refused to do, except in one or two special cases, namely to invite outside assistance in their organization, it seems to me that the
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell matter is hopeless. I am therefore not giving a lot of detailed cases of expenditure.
When even the ministers are admitting that things are uncertain and that we are maybe running into difficulties, I confess that I would have thought that this would have been a time for retrenchment, but I have seen no sign of it; there is no sign of it. It would look as if the government has no capacity to deal with this matter. Apparently, something comes over men when they have been a long time in power, and they do not seem to reach the conclusions that sensible men would reach in their own business or which I assume the members of the government reach in dealing with their own affairs. But when you find that nondefence expenditures are up by hundreds of millions of dollars, it really causes you to think. Of course, in a private organization that kind of thing could not happen. There would be the acid test of the profit and loss account. I confess that I had thought that even the government, faced with a situation which has been partially disclosed to us, would have taken some steps to deal with it; but as I say, I can find no sign of it whatever.
The leader of my party, who incidentally has had a great deal of experience of government, has made suggestions with regard to calling in outside assistance, and the answer has been in the negative. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) dealt with this matter at considerable length and his refusal took two lines, first that there was nothing to correct and, second, that if there were a report such as that which was made by the Hoover commission, it would do no good. The arguments which were used I found to be very strange and 1 propose to deal with them at some little length because I regard this as a matter of first-class importance; and if it is possible that anything I shall say will have any effect on the decision, I want to say it.
The first argument used by the minister I thought was extremely strange. He pointed out what is true, namely that our cabinet comes into being in a different way from that of the cabinet in the United States where, as we know, members of the cabinet are named by the president. He seemed to think that because the government obtained its authority from the votes of the people, unlike the government in the United States which is appointed by the president, that fact was going to make all the difference in the world. I find his argument interesting,
3986	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell unusual and, if I might say so without being offensive, nonsensical. Here it is. The minister first says:
These men-
That is, the members of the Canadian cabinet.
-take an oath of office that they will carry out the specific work that has been assigned to them.
By that remark the minister seems to imply that by taking the oath of office people, regardless of their capacity or their experience, by some magic have become supremely or absolutely competent to do their job. The minister goes on to say this, and what he says is quite unwarranted:
We are asked now to accept the view that these men are mediocre people, and very bad administrators.
Nobody has used harsh words of that kind. There has been no suggestion of that kind. The suggestion has been that there was room for assistance from outside. Nobody knows better than does the Minister of Trade and Commerce that, in the business world, it is those who are most competent who are most ready to call in outside assistance.
Then next the minister says this-

speechtext:
I am confident that it is a previous session. The next thing we have is this:
We are asked to get a group of Independent people, as though there were no independence in those administering the affairs of government.
I find myself unable to think of the right word by means of which to describe this argument. I will reply to it merely by asking a question of the minister. When it was found necessary for the Post Office Department to get an outside report-which I understand was before the regime of the present Postmaster General (Mr. Cote)-did the government ask a member of the government to do it or did they get someone from outside? We all know the answer. Therefore the government's action really makes absurd the answer given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I am dwelling on this matter, Mr. Speaker, because it seems to me a striking and almost
IMr. Macdonnell.]

unbelievable instance of the complete, impenetrable and absurd self-satisfaction of the government. The minister repudiated the idea that anyone from outside could help. He said:
I presume that the government would choose the very best men they could find, but the fact that it would be an independent body without responsibility to anyone would be, in my opinion, no guarantee that they would be better judges of how this parliamentary government should be organized and administered than are the elected representatives of the people who have sworn to carry out that particular task.
Again you see, Mr. Speaker, the belief in the mythical effect of taking an oath. I will not embarrass the minister by asking him if it is really true that in the case of all his colleagues the oath has covered all defects of mind and heart, and whether he has found them all the supermen we are now asked to consider them.
Now, the minister goes on and says that he has not heard of any great changes being made as a result of the Hoover report. To that I would answer that I commend to the minister a publication entitled "Status of the Hoover Report", by a committee of citizens. It is further called, "A citizen's guide to the progress of Federal Reorganization". It is worth setting out some of the conditions which the Hoover commission found when they began to delve into the Washington situation, because I assume we will not be stupid enough to imagine similar conditions would not be found here.
I shall recite some of the incidents upon which the Hoover commission reported. One Missouri farmer received conflicting advice on the use of fertilizer from five separate agencies in the Department of Agriculture. It would not be hard to imagine, with all the economists we have in our own department, that there might occasionally be duplication in our Department of Agriculture. Budgeting and accounting-the government was maintaining four separate distinct and duplicate sets of books for some important types of federal accounting. Because of obsolete laws, freight car loads of old vouchers were being shipped to Washington for detailed audit when a simple spot check in the field would suffice. Labour -there were more federal activities outside the Department of Labour than in it. This reminds one, incidentally, of our own Department of Trade and Commerce producing unemployment figures as far apart as the poles from those of the Department of Labour. Indian affairs-there were 12,000 Indian bureau employees administering the affairs of 393,000 Indians, or one federal employee to each 32 Indians. Medical activities-five large and thirty smaller hospital systems

went their separate ways "with little knowledge and no regard for" one another's operations. New hospitals were sometimes built in areas where others stood empty. Others were built in remote places where neither patients nor physicians could use them.
Does anyone believe that if an expert reviewing agency reviewed our affairs it would fail to find similar situations? If anyone does, let him look at the Woods-Gordon report on the post office. 1 quote the following from page 42 of that report:
The "Primary Sortation" is the first division of unsorted mail into a number of different groups. While this plan will require further development, there is an indicated annual saving in the forward letter section of the Toronto post office alone of approximately $200,000 per annum.
I quote again from page 54:
While these suggested revisions in the organization's structure in the transportation branch do not materially change the administrative functions they strike at the primary weakness, the lack of future policy and program regarding the extent and nature of transportation services.
To suggest in the face of this that there is no need of inquiry and investigation does not make sense. It will merely create the impression the government is not happy about the situation and that there are things to hide.
It only remains to add that the story of the results of the Hoover commission does not in the least warrant the suggestion it has been ineffective. Here is a summary which is illuminating. The recommendations made by the commission totalled 273. Of these 116 or 42 per cent have been accomplished; 35 or 12 per cent have been mostly accomplished; 44 or 16 per cent have been partially accomplished, which leaves 77 out of 273 remaining.
I do not think, in the light of this, anyone will seriously say that the Hoover report should be laughed off. Of course, it has been hard, when everything has been booming, to get the public interested, but it may be more easy to interest them in the future than it is now. The government is content to advise other people to reduce their expenses, but they do not set an example. Indeed, of course, the government makes it almost impossible for other people to reduce their costs by maintaining taxation at such a rate.
I come now to the question of unemployment. There is nothing in the budget to comfort the unemployed except the minister's optimism, which is a thin mixture. However, I believe the unemployed should turn their wrath rather on the Minister of Trade and Commerce than on the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Trade and Commerce
12, 1954
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell manages to ignore the figures which come from the Department of Labour. He runs an opposition show of his own. The confusion really becomes complete when the two departments use different words to describe unemployment. It is a kind of runaround. "Unplaced applicants", as they are called by the Department of Labour, are not far from 100 per cent higher than the "persons without jobs and seeking work", which is the phrase produced by the trade and commerce department and used by its minister. Then, we have a third category of "persons without jobs and seeking work, plus persons on temporary layoff".
Here are the latest figures available as at February 20 last. Unplaced applicants, in round figures, totalled 559,000. This is the figure published by the Department of Labour, but the dominion bureau of statistics produces an entirely different figure for "persons without jobs and seeking work, 312,000". To add to the confusion, there is the third figure entitled "persons without jobs and seeking work, plus persons on temporary layoff, 335,000". We have, as I say, complete confusion. We have the government speaking with two if not three voices, and the confusion gets worse the farther we go.
In speaking about this the Minister of Finance says, as reported at page 3727 of Hansard for April 6, 1954:
And I do not believe, in any case, that increased public works of the kind appropriate for the federal government can remedy a problem which is to a large extent local in character.
Now, the word "local" attracted me because I think the minister has failed entirely to keep in touch with the labour department. The March issue of the Labour Gazette shows an average of 40 per cent of Canadian wage and salary earners in what is called "substantial labour surplus areas", and almost all the rest in moderate surplus areas. To put it differently, may I say that of 109 localities, 57 were in substantial surplus, 48 in moderate surplus, and only four very small places were in approximate balance of labour demand and labour supply. In percentage figures what this means is that in more than half the area there was at least one worker in every ten unemployed, and in practically all the other areas from one in ten or one in sixteen were unemployed.
In the face of this situation, what comfort are the unemployed to get? All that they have is what the Winnipeg Free Press calls "the surprisingly buoyant assumption that the upturn in the second half of the present year will more than compensate for the declines which have been evident in certain branches of industry since the beginning of
3988	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell the year." Now, the minister says again, at page 3726 of Hansard for the same date:
Indeed, in the dynamic kind of economy we have in Canada an occasional hesitation in its forward movement may well be one of the consequences of the buoyant character of our economic growth.
"Occasional hesitation"-I think that will seem, to the man who is suffering from unemployment, like a far-off distant voice of some superior being to whom the affairs of poor mortal men are remote. "Occasional hesitation", however, will mean something very real and vital to the unemployed in their day-to-day lives.
The ministers tosses the ball lightly from one to the other. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) says the time has not come for public works, and that the Minister of Finance will deal with the situation by fiscal and monetary measures. The Minister of Finance seems to be in the same mood he was in earlier in the year when he said that unemployment was not really "serious", although he admitted that it was "unpleasant". Having got himself to this point, his conclusion is not surprising. He said:
In the light of all these considerations I do not feel that drastic measures by government are appropriate to the present economic situation. Governmental intervention or expenditure is not a cure for the problem of those industries where supply has temporarily outrun demand.
The ministers are good at negation. "It is not time for this". "It is not time for that". What is it time for? We get nothing but negation, and the hope that the United States will cure our problem. That is really all that is left.
I should qualify that to this extent, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce speaking the other day in Toronto, did seem to have a vague idea that not everything was quite right. He did say that there would be cooperation between government and industry with regard to employment. But he did not seem to worry about it, at all. His conclusion was:
By and large, the Canadian economy remains buoyant and expanding.
Of course everyone hopes that the ministers are right. The Minister of Finance is pinning his hopes on United States recovery. But we must, incidentally, remind ministers that costs must come down, and that blithely offering cheap advice to producers about costs, while the government does not do anything about it, leaves them in the very greatest of difficulty.
What the unemployed make of all this, I cannot say. When ministers are not agreed on the problem, how is it likely that the


unemployed will feel when there is no serious interest being taken? And when other ministers ignore the Minister of Labour, how can the unemployed have confidence? It is too much to expect. If uncalculated optimism blunders into being right, well and good. But supposing this optimism is wrong-then we will be in a proper mess, and the government will be responsible for taking the risk, which the Financial Times says is a "calculated risk", but which in my opinion is wishful thinking.
I have been talking about the unemployed. Their plight is largely caused by shrinkage in our export trade, and I now propose to say a few words about trade, including the subject of wheat. The Minister of Finance spoke hopefully about international organizations which have to do with international trade. He mentioned the international monetary fund, the organization for European economic co-operation, and the general agreement on tariffs and trade. And we can all hope that his expectations will be realized. But again I say that he cannot take advantage of these conditions, however important they may be, unless we have set our own house in order, and can meet competitive prices.
The Toronto Star draws this warning from what the minister said, when it says:
Our economic growth has slowed to a walk.
And again:
It may not be necessary, as Mr. Abbott says, for the government to take any drastic measures to deal with the recession. But even if business recovers to last year's levels it will not give us the expanding economy we need to sustain full production and employment.
I suggest that is a remark well worth pondering, because it is true our economic activities these last few years have depended upon a constantly expanding economy. In the atmosphere which has been created, to stop expanding is going to mean the equivalent of going backward, because so many people have come to count on expansion as the ordinary course of things; to believe that next year will be better than this, and to arrange their expenditures accordingly. Indeed, I think we can say that the government has, in effect done that. And it is not surprising that the ordinary citizen has followed their lead.
So the condition we have is that the government is gambling with the welfare of the unemployed, and indeed with the welfare of all of us. I shall not worry hon. members with long details of trade figures. I could point out that in 1953 we had a trade deficit of $210 million against a surplus of $325 million the year before, or a net worsening of $535 million.

The reasons are three in number. The first of these is the premium on the Canadian dollar, which impeded trade to some extent. The second is the price of Canadian goods and the third the shortage of dollars in certain areas.
As regards the prices of Canadian goods I wish to remind hon. members of a comment which has been quoted in the house- and, Mr. Speaker, I am not quoting from the press, but rather from the speech at the annual meeting of the Royal Bank where Mr. Muir said:
Startling and unpleasant as it may be, there is evidence that Canada is tending to become a high cost economy in which natural and artificial barriers prevent us from achieving the degree of flexibility and mobility required for orderly adjustment.
Now, I have spoken about the decline in foreign trade, caused increasingly I think by our high costs and our failure to meet competition abroad, which is disconcerting enough. But, worse still-and there is plenty of evidence of it-is the failure to meet competition at home. Mr. Forsyth, president of Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, has spoken recently of the failure to meet competition "in our own backyard." He no doubt had in mind cases of Canadian manufacturers being substantially undersold by European competitors, particularly those from the United Kingdom. Two recent cases have come to my own attention, in one of which a United Kingdom competitor tenderer 50 per cent below the Canadian tenderer and in another case 22 per cent below.
Of course we all know the results of German competition because there is much of it. Particularly, with our own eyes, we see the little German motor car, the Volkswagen, on our streets.
What does the Minister of Finance say about all this? Well, he seems to be doing a kind of balancing act. On the one hand, in a realistic passage of his speech he says:
Some industries are finding that they have not watched their costs as carefully as they should, that their break-even points are uncomfortably high, and that their costs and prices are out of line.
And again he says:
The re-emergence of keen competition in trade means readjustment and appraisal.
But in the next breath we have:
I do not believe that the current slowing down of expansion will be serious or prolonged.
Then he comforts himself by saying:
Responsible opinion in the United States seems to be confident that the present down-turn will not be deep or prolonged.
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
And finally he has persuaded himself by his own optimistic arguments when he says:
I think an up-swing in the second half of the year will more than compensate for the declines that are evident in certain branches of industry at present.
I think it would have been more accurate if the minister had said, not "I think" but "I want to think" or "I must think" or "I am determined to think".
While I am speaking about export sales I should like to say a word about wheat. Apart from the large amount involved, wheat has always been regarded as a kind of index of the Canadian economy. The many inquiries made in the house the Minister of Trade and Commerce was apt to wave aside rather airily, and to suggest there was nothing much to be concerned about. But I do not think the position of the farmers warrants his unconcern. The net income of farmers was down 14 per cent in 1953 from 1952, and more than 23 per cent from 1951, while the index of the things the farmer buys shows that it is down only 4 per cent.
I think the seriousness of the situation struck the house and the country suddenly about a month ago when the minister told us that no wheat from the 1953 crop was yet sold, and that on January 30 there were 127 million bushels from the 1952 crop in the hands of the wheat board. On January 30, 127 million bushels from the 1952 crop were in the wheat board's hands. The situation on March 24, I am informed, was that 359 million bushels were in commercial positions, and 328 million bushels estimated deliverable on farms, making a total of 687 million bushels.
If the disappearance in the last four months of the crop year is 35 million bushels a month, which I understand is favourable, it would leave us about 550 million bushels on July 31, which is only six weeks away from the delivery of the 1954 crop. Notwithstanding this very high supply position, the Canadian government has taken what competent people regard as the very speculative, long position. It seems perfectly clear that if we have another good crop this position will almost certainly cost Canada dearly.
Those who are interested in precedents carry their minds back to a similar situation existing in 1929. At that time the pool virtually tried to hold up European purchasers and it had what we have learned to call a chain effect on shipping and other things, and was one of the things that precipitated the unfortunate situation that descended on us then.
I suggest that there should be some cooperation, a meeting of minds between the

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is constantly telling us we are very fortunate to have that wheat just as wheat, and says you cannot go wrong as long as you hold wheat. There are some others in this house who have a mercenary idea that wheat is for the purpose of being sold, and they do not all seem to agree with the minister; however, I am not quoting them because their views will not prevail very far. But I do think that the Minister of Trade and Commerce ought to try to persuade the Minister of Agriculture. There does not seem to be unanimity there.

There seems to me at the moment no question of international aid; the question is about selling wheat in a competitive market, and without pretending to adjudicate between two such experts as the two right hon. gentlemen, I have a feeling that the Minister of Agriculture has had quite a lot of experience in selling wheat, but maybe he will want to correct that, too.

The Minister ol Trade and Commerce is a man of many devices, but whether he is good at salesmanship is something that I do not know. Of course his experience with the grain business had nothing to do with selling; it had to do only with storing, and I am wondering whether he has a complex; whether he has got very, very good at storing and not much good at selling, and whether he gets great pleasure out of having bursting elevators all across the country-very well built by him. There was one unfortunate instance that we were told of the other night where one of the C.C.F. members nearly met his end, which would have deprived us of the pleasure of meeting him. At any rate, that is a long time ago. But it seems to me, when we have all this wheat and the minister sitting on top of it, the question does arise whether we are in a good position or not.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has always been a great perplexity to me because he says-and I am sure he says it sincerely- that he is a believer in private enterprise. I have no reason to doubt that, except there are so many things he does that seem utterly inconsistent with it. Here we have a situation where the minister tells us we have got to rely on the good judgment of the wheat board. I have no doubt that the wheat board, if we could get inside their minds, would say; Of course we have to rely on the judgment of the minister. At any rate, between them they arrive at conclusions, and in any event it is the judgment of a small group of men; and this minister, who is a great exponent of private enterprise, is on the other hand so keen on having control in his own hands that we do not really get the benefits of private enterprise in anything that he gets hold of by way of public enterprise. Therefore I think it is legitimate to ask-I have no expert knowledge to do more than ask-whether it is possible that a few men who are now in control of selling wheat are backing their judgment against experienced purchasers in Europe. If they are, the question further arises whether they have open minds to believe that the situation is changing. Do not let us forget that the present handling of wheat has deprived us of merchandising skill. My friends to the left, even if they listen to what I say, will disapprove entirely of what I say. We are deprived of the judgment of scores or hundreds of expert 83276-2524
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell merchandisers backing their judgment against each other and each day reaching what is the best composite view as to what price wheat can be sold at.

speechtext:
I am not making any suggestions except that I hope that the minister is not going to leave us in the position we are in now. The well-informed and always moderate review of the Bank of Nova Scotia for March has this important thing to say:
The piling up of wheat stocks, not only in Canada but in the United States, the current restrictions on United States wheat acreage, the slow rate of sales under the international wheat agreement this season, the year-long decline in wheat prices outside the agreement and the recent seven-cent reduction in the Canadian lakehead price, are all symptomatic of the changed atmosphere. The world wheat market has become much more competitive . . . world trade in wheat will likely be smaller this year, and there is much to suggest that North American exports will bear more than their share of the decline.
Again the writer says:
The combination of increased supplies and lessened demand has brought about a striking change in the atmosphere of the world wheat market. This change is clearly reflected in the slow movement of wheat under the international wheat agreement. Up to mid-February only a little more than 35 per cent of the amount of wheat which the four participating exporters agreed to sell and the 45 participating importers to buy in 1953-54, had been sold. And it should be noted that the total commitment under the agreement this season, because of the failure of the United Kingdom to enter, amounts only to 421 million bushels. At the corresponding date in each of the two preceding seasons, at least 70 per cent of the annual amount of 581 million bushels then covered by the agreement had been sold.
Later it has this to say:
Though the policy of the wheat board is to keep. Canadian prices fully competitive, there seems to. be no disposition to pursue an aggressive policy of price reduction.
Finally:
Regardless of how well prices hold up during the remainder of the season there is no doubt that the more competitive wheat market and the mounting surplus make the outlook for Canadian wheat more uncertain than it has been for a long time.
The matter could hardly be in a more unsatisfactory position. The minister gives us the bland assurance that wheat is a good asset. As time passes the minister takes things more and more into his own hands, and instead of obtaining the best composite judgment we can have we have to rely on him. Attempts were made to hold up the purchases in the United States and Canada in 1929 but they failed. As I said, there was

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell a chain reaction on shipping and other business. There is a vast difference between the situation today and in 1929 but enough similarity to make us think.
Outside North American markets, wheat is becoming more competitive than for a good many years and purchasers are in a stronger position. Is the wheat board following the example of the Minister of Finance and relying on the hope that all will be well? Are they taking a gamble hoping that they can make the purchaser dance to their tune? Is there in the backs of their minds the feeling that if things turn bad they will be able to deposit the problem on the doorstep of the government?
One thing is certain, that others are suffering. Lake shippers are facing a serious situation and ocean shippers too. Up to a few weeks ago little or no wheat had been booked for shipping via the St. Lawrence this season, something almost unprecedented. Freight ships have left Saint John virtually empty.
I have been talking about trade, notably wheat. I wish now to say a few words about competitive costs, taxation and inflation. We are collecting $1,200 million from corporations by way of income tax. This means $1,200 million added to production costs. It is conceded by every reputable authority that the best way to revive purchasing power is to reduce taxation. Of course, in addition to the taxes on corporations we take approximately $1,200 million income tax from individuals, and there are other taxes direct and indirect. When ministers advise us to cut down costs but can do nothing to assist by reducing taxes it is really preaching to the air. The position in which exporters are going to find themselves, if there is no means of cutting down their costs by tax reduction, may be a very serious situation indeed.
I want to say a word about monetary policy. We have had fifteen years of boom stimulated by the government's financial policy. In 1946 the government feared a recession, and at that time they took action to stimulate when it was proper, but since then they have been trying to eat their cake and have it by stimulating purchasing power and at the same time, as in 1946 and 1947, trying by financial measures to avoid rising prices. This proved largely ineffective, and it is essential to recall that while prices were rising the government was artificially stimulating investment through double depreciation.
Reviewing the intervening years quickly, in 1950 the boom which had existed slackened slightly and there was fear of unemployment. Then came the Korean war which stimulated the boom to still further heights. In the
IMr. Macdonnell.]

spring of 1951 the government did take steps to curb, but their courage deserted them in 1952 under pressure, and again they abandoned restraining measures. Instead of moderation the government stoked up the boom. The gross national product kept mounting until it was $24-3 billion in 1953, 33 per cent higher than in 1950, and 75 per cent higher than in 1946. Now the rate of expansion has slowed, perhaps to a walk.
In 1952 the gross national product was 7 per cent ahead of 1951. Last year the increase was 5 per cent and this year it is expected to be not more than 3 per cent. We must remember of course that inflation has always been very attractive to the government because it has enabled them to spend more and still have surpluses, but this built-in inflation, as it has been well called, of high taxes will take a lot of readjustment. As I said earlier, anything short of a roaring boom in the mentality which we have developed is going to be hard to live with.
I shall not detain the house longer on inflation, but we should not forget its danger merely because it has been living with us for a long time. Some well-informed people believe that the recent call for redemption of $2 billion of government bonds indicates a new voyage into inflation. The Republican administration in the United States came into power with a great blowing of trumpets pledged to hard money, so-called honest money. Now they have done a right-about-face and with the fear of the November election they are pursuing a soft-money policy. They are trying to give the economy stimulation by cheap money and low interest rates, in other words, another dose of inflation.
I do hope this operation of our finance department is not the signal for us to start in on a debasement of the currency with all that it means in the way of high prices and other unfortunate results. I end, Mr. Speaker, where I began, with a list of the negations of which the budget consists: Nothing done for employment; nothing real done to relieve the taxpayer; nothing done to break the deadlock in wheat; nothing done to indicate any intention of improving the efficiency of government; and nothing done to reassure us that we are not going to have another spate of inflation. It is a dismal recital of hopes, vague optimism and admonitions to others to do things when the government itself seems helpless to do anything. I move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that the government
(a)	has failed to reduce taxes which are an

excessive burden on the Canadian people and place our producers under a severe disadvantage in meeting competition from abroad;
(b)	has failed to reduce unnecessary expenditure;
(c)	has failed to improve the efficiency of its administration;
(d)	ignores the problem of unemployment;
(e)	has failed to retain and regain markets for our surplus primary products;
(f)	has failed to reach agreement with the provincial governments in regard to a clearly defined reallocation of taxing powers so that the provincial governments and municipal councils may have adequate financial resources to carry out their rapidly-increasing responsibilities."

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will understand if I do not discuss the various suggestions, proposals and criticisms made in the amendment which has just been moved. In his address the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) dwelt at some considerable length on some topics with which I would also like to deal at some length, the most notable being the problem of marketing our farm produce and wheat. However, since that is a matter which should be the subject of extended consideration I do nbt propose to deal with it. I shall leave that to one or more of my colleagues who are familiar with the wheat situation in western Canada. However, I do wish to say something about the budget and the speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) made when he introduced his budget.
The minister has, as usual, given an interesting and optimistic review of the Canadian economy and its prospects for the current financial year. Time alone will tell whether his optimism-which my hon. friend calls wishful thinking and I suppose optimism is closely allied to wishful thinking-is justified or not; but I am sure that people generally believe that the outlook is not nearly as rosy or as encouraging as he painted it.
As the minister spoke, more than 500,000 people in Canada were registered as seeking jobs; and on the farms the impact of falling prices has already been felt. The farmers in western Canada, as we have been told, have a vast accumulation of grain, and the marketing prospects are far from bright. Some farmers, including some in my own constituency, had little or no crop in 1952, and the failure to market or make arrangements for advance payments on any part of the 1953 crop, which could not be marketed because of the quota, has caused difficulty and stress.
Taking into account those considerations, I believe the minister is unduly optimistic. He indicated, too, that the gross national product for 1954 will be much the same as
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell in 1953. He appeared to be satisfied with that position. But I would point out that, unless our gross national product increases at a greater rate than our increasing population and in accordance with the technological improvements which are made from time to time, the problem of employment will become increasingly difficult. If the gross national product in 1954 remains at the same level as in 1953, it should be clear that there will be no improvement in the employment situation in Canada next autumn and winter, although activity in the coming spring and the summer should give us some temporary relief.
The budget then, in our opinion, fails to take any decisive action to meet the two problems to which I have referred. They are the two important and urgent problems of maintaining full employment, to which we are committed under the charter of the United Nations, and the improvement in the agricultural industry.
It seems to me that now is the time, when the budget is being introduced, to outline some positive steps to improve these conditions. I believe the minister failed to do this. Budgetary steps should have been taken to increase the purchasing power of the average Canadian so as to enlarge the domestic demand for the larger product which we can produce. That could have been done, Mr. Speaker, in several ways. Among them and coming immediately to mind should have been an increase in the exemptions under the Income Tax Act to those taxpayers in the lower brackets. I am not urging any relief in corporation taxes. With the high rents and high prices for clothing and other commodities which enter into the cost of living, steps should be taken to relieve the small taxpayers of impositions that were placed upon them when the cost of living was appreciably lower. We have urged before and I do so again that exemptions for single persons should be raised to $1,500 and for married couples to $3,000.
The minister, in effect, echoed complaints that the old age security plan was becoming an increasing burden on our budget. These payments are like family allowances and unemployment insurance. They are means of redistributing the national income and maintaining the purchasing power among our people. They are, in effect, insurance premiums against depression and are therefore, in my opinion, legitimate impositions on our people as a whole. One means, of course, of improving the position of the old age security fund would be to remove the ceiling on the two per cent levy which is now limited to a
3994	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell maximum of $60 per individual taxpayer. The removal of this ceiling would be a step in the direction of levying the contribution according to the ability to pay. I believe that levying according to the ability to pay is the kind of levy that is favoured by most people today.
Then, too, there should have been much more of a reduction in excise and sales taxes. Some excise taxes were reduced but they affect a relatively small number of items and I do not think they will be felt at the level of the consumer. Sales taxes are the most regressive form of taxation. Where they are used in the provinces they are used of necessity to meet social services which, we believe, should be the responsibility of this parliament through a national social security plan, a plan that was proposed by the government in 1945 at the dominion-provincial conference of that year. Sales taxes are a tax on purchasing power and thus not only reduce the ability to buy goods to the amount of the tax, but discourage people from buying in the domestic market upon which we must depend more and more as time passes. This discouragement is felt particularly by the great mass of the people whose purchasing power, individually, is low, but in aggregate, represents the bulk of the buying of consumer goods in this or any other country. Moreover, the new exemptions under the sales tax and excise taxes, reduced or repealed, relate to many articles which may be deemed luxury goods, such as jewelry, diamonds, semi-precious stones, cut glass, and articles of that description.
I should immediately say, however, that I wish to commend the minister in one particular and that is for the exemptions under the sales tax on equipment sold to, or imported by, municipalities, especially designed for road making, fire-fighting and so on. But I regret that this does not include motor trucks, which represent a heavy cost to municipal governments. It is regrettable that household necessities, such as children's clothes and babies' shoes, are still taxed. This emphasizes the point that the tax reductions or exemptions have been made in many instances on the wrong item.
Because of the government's failure to take what I have termed positive action, and which would meet the general economic recession which has manifested itself during the past few months, the pressure has been growing on this parliament to take a negative kind of action. By this I mean that there have been increasing demands for protection through higher tariffs for certain industries which have been feeling the effects of the economic recession.

I want to say immediately that we of the C.C.F. have often urged general economic policies to meet the needs of the economy generally, but I do not propose to recite them at length today. Most of them were very clearly developed by my colleagues in the recent debate on unemployment. In effect, by refusing to plan actively for full employment and for more stability in agricultural prices, there has been strong pressure for increased tariff protection which, in his budget speech, I am glad to say the minister felt compelled to refuse. I should like to say to him that we in this group stand for the principles of freer trade among the nations. We believe that the welfare of Canada depends not only on intelligent trade relationships providing opportunity for our entry into world markets, but that this opportunity can only be provided to our producers to the extent that we are prepared to accept goods in exchange for the goods that we sell abroad.
I found it difficult to follow the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to the effect that the United States has been somewhat at least of a champion of freer trade. Personally, I have not seen any clear evidence of this in their actions, though many speeches have been made by prominent Americans, including the President, seeking to convey that impression. There is an old proverb which says, "Actions speak louder than words". The minister's statement came very soon after the latest breach, on the part of the United States, of the Geneva agreement on tariffs and trade by way of new restrictions on the importation of Canadian barley. I should like to say that I was disappointed, when this matter was drawn to the attention of the house, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) felt that this breach of GATT did not require an emphatic protest from our government. This was particularly the case because it is only the latest in a series of unilateral actions on the part of the United States which emphasizes the uncertainties of United States markets for Canadian produce and goods.

Yes. I thank the minister for the correction. It is because of this uncertainty that we have been urging the government to endeavour, in a more positive fashion, to encourage trade with nations other than the United States, more particularly, of course, with the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries.
'Mr. Coldwell.]

The budget, I say, made few reductions in what I have called regressive taxes or indeed in any other form of taxation. I have noted before that both the United States and the United Kingdom have outlined some reductions in their defence expenditures. I feel that with the relaxation in world tension we could safely reduce our defence expenditures, as the United States has done, by at least 10 per cent this year. I am sure that our people cannot look happily upon suggestions that it may be necessary to maintain indefinitely that drain upon our national expenditures to the extent of some 43 per cent of the national budget. I want to emphasize once again that the strength of Canada and that of the democratic world rests not so much on a high level of armaments-although again I reiterate that defence expenditures are necessary in the kind of world in which we are living today-but that true defence will lie in the feeling of the mass of the people that the needs of themselves and their families are being adequately met by national policies as far as they affect our national economy.
There are indeed many worth-while social security measures that Canadians themselves must have in order to maintain and improve their standards as a modern, democratic and progressive people. To the extent that we can move in that direction, and indeed assist other peoples in the world to move in the same direction-and I think that is equally important-to that extent can we reduce and finally, we hope, eliminate the present threats of totalitarianism whether of the fascist or communist variety. Let us bear in mind that the threat to freedom in the world is not only from communist sources but from varieties of fascism here and there across the world. Thus, I want to suggest once again that since the new and frightful weapons of war make most types of military equipment for our forces obsolete, we should do everything possible to assist in reaching universal agreements for progressive disarmament and thus to be able to divert a substantial part of our defence appropriations to giving material and-what is perhaps more important- technical aid to underprivileged and underdeveloped peoples and areas everywhere. I want to say that this, in our opinion, is the only sure way of promoting the peaceful progress of mankind.
Among measures that are required to strengthen our own economy and to avert serious distress are not only projects like a national health plan-which I would place at the very top of our requirements in the realm of social security legislation-improvement in family allowances, old age pensions,
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell unemployment benefits, crop insurance and so on, but economic undertakings-because, after all, if we are going to have the kind of social security that we envisage, we must have an economic basis that will carry the social security system-that will bolster the economy in vulnerable areas and increase production to enhance our gross national product. Among these are, of course, projects like the St. Lawrence seaway project and irrigation projects. Among the latter, first and foremost, is the utilization of the waters of our great rivers, particularly those of the South Saskatchewan river.
I am sure hon. members will pardon me if I refer to this particular project for a few moments at this time because, as a matter of fact, my own constituency is both sides of this river and the undertaking of that irrigation project would affect my constituency more than any other one in the province of Saskatchewan. Those of us who, like myself, can remember the years of drought and disaster over large areas of otherwise fertile land on both sides of this river are most anxious to see this project undertaken. 1 do not propose this afternoon to outline the tortuous statements made in Saskatchewan by supporters of the federal government regarding this project or to discuss the varying estimates of cost that have been produced by the federal government from time to time, it seemed to many of us, to delay the carrying out of this important project. I think this is clearly outlined in the record of correspondence over the years between the federal government and the provincial government of Saskatchewan. I think that an examination of the correspondence and statements indicates that the federal government has been vague and, if I may use the term, somewhat evasive.
I know, of course, that the present government of Saskatchewan has never asked the federal government to subsidize the generation of electric power. It has been clear, I think, that the provincial government has been prepared to contribute to the construction of the dam the same amount of money that it would cost the province to generate the potential power in some other manner. There are two sides to this question but no one, I think, would suggest that the users of power in the province of Saskatchewan should be asked to subsidize an irrigation and water conservation project which is the responsibility, in my opinion, of the federal government and which it has assumed elsewhere. It seems to me that the time has come when, instead of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner)-whom I am glad to see in his seat this afternoon-presenting his

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell views to the government of Saskatchewan, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)-and I am glad to see him here to hear this suggestion-and the federal government should be prepared to state that they are prepared to undertake the project on a fair and equitable basis and, I hope, to undertake it within a very short time. Negotiations have been conducted, it has appeared to me, in the hope that by driving an increasingly hard bargain the provincial government can be forced to reject federal proposals in the hope that blame for any failure to proceed will fall upon the provincial government. The difficulty has been that, even when the Saskatchewan government has been willing to make an agreement along lines suggested by the Minister of Agriculture, he has always been in the position of being able to say that for various reasons the federal government has decided not to proceed with the undertaking at the time.
1 think it is unfair to ask one party to carry on negotiations with the knowledge that any firm commitments made by the province are regarded as binding, whereas any commitment which the Minister of Agriculture or his officials may make is done with a clear understanding that the federal government is not yet committed to proceed, even though a satisfactory agreement may be reached by a joint committee of the P.F.R.A., acting on behalf of the federal government, and by representatives of the provincial administration.
As I have said, what is required is a firm statement from the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that this government intends to proceed with the dam in the event of a satisfactory agreement being reached between the two governments regarding the divisions of costs. The time has arrived, indeed has long since passed, when the provincial government should not be expected to negotiate on a purely hypothetical basis, not knowing whether they are being merely manoeuvred into rejecting an impossible agreement, and without any assurance that if a satisfactory agreement regarding division of costs is worked out the whole thing may not be rejected in the final stages by the federal government. To those of us who represent constituencies which may become once again stricken by dry years and drought, this project is of primary interest and importance; but more than that it is of fundamental interest to the economy of Canada and to all the people of Canada. I want to emphasize this in view of the tremendous cost of the relief that had to be poured into these areas because of the prolonged drought in the thirties.
'Mr. Coldwell. 3

Mention of this dominion-provincial project leads me to comment on the finance minister's forthright statement declining to allow the deduction from federal income taxes of the new 15 per cent personal income tax in Quebec beyond the present limit of 5 per cent. I recognize at once that, under our constitution, a province has the right to impose a direct tax, such as the income tax, if it chooses to do so. But it is equally clear, I believe, that the federal parliament also has a constitutional right in this field. The doctrine that the provinces have priority in the field of direct taxation and that the federal government should, in effect, move over to the extent that the provinces decide, is a dangerous, insidious and false doctrine that could not, under any circumstances I believe, be supported by any member in this house. We must always remember that the people of the provinces are represented in the federal parliament as well as in the provincial legislatures.
We in this group believe in our federal system and want to preserve it. We want to preserve the rights of this parliament. We want to preserve the autonomy of the provinces in the fields in which they are granted complete sovereignty and autonomy. In the past, we had given our support to the federal-provincial tax rental agreements because we believed that they best served the interests of all the people of Canada by assuring all provincial governments of more adequate revenue to administer their provincial programs in their own way and under their own authority, while at the same time assuring the federal government the necessary fiscal powers to develop social security and other policies that will benefit Canadians generally wherever they may live, and tend to spread more adequately the burden of taxation in all parts of Canada.
In saying this and taking issue with the demand of the premier of Quebec, I want to make it very clear that in his activities over the past few years in promoting the fallacious idea that Canada is less a nation than an association of ten sovereign states, with the assumption by the premier of Quebec of the right to pass legislation often incompatible with the fundamental democratic rights of Canadian citizens, he has merely carried forward the type of propaganda used for many years by the Liberal party in Quebec to further its own political interests. In other words, in my view, to some extent these are chickens coming home to roost. I do not propose to elaborate upon this to any extent at the moment, but the pages of Hansard as well as the public press will vindicate the view I have just expressed.

In the recent past the federal government neglected to protect Canadian civil rights when the padlock law was passed, and most recently when the freedom of worship act was amended by the Quebec legislature. I know this act was directed against a sect with whose teachings and with whose type of propaganda I have no sympathy whatever, but that legislation could be used to curtail other religious rights and freedoms of other religious denominations and minorities in Quebec. I want to emphasize that throughout the years the propaganda of the Liberal party, both provincial and national, prepared the groundwork for this ultra-nationalism and the claims of Mr. Duplessis. The Liberal party of Canada, I repeat, as well as the Liberal party of Quebec, must bear the grave responsibility for paving the way for what is today an attack, and a very threatening and insidious attack, on Canadian unity and our general national welfare.
Let me say again that we believe in the federal system. We desire to see all the provinces of Canada able to carry out their constitutional functions without interference by this federal parliament. We believe that, in order to achieve this purpose, the tax rental agreements are of primary importance and concern to the welfare and autonomy of the provinces of Canada, particularly of the less favoured provinces. Let me say, however, to the federal government that it must not forget its own proposals to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction in 1945, which included more than these fiscal arrangements. The terms on which the federal government asked the provinces to release certain tax fields, including that of personal income tax, which incidentally some of them including Quebec and Ontario had only begun to enter, comprised not only rental payments but undertakings by the federal government to do things that would ease the financial burdens of the provinces. I believe Quebec did not impose a personal income tax until 1939, and then had it in effect for only two years.
Among these proposals was complete responsibility for adequate old age pensions at the age of 70 without a means test, and half the cost of old age assistance for persons between 65 and 69. No one will argue today that $40 per month is adequate. There was, too, the proposal to assume full responsibility for assistance to the employable unemployed. Most important of all, there was the proposal to introduce a national system of health insurance to give complete health coverage to the people of Canada. On 83276-253
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell the economic side the federal authority proposed a public investment policy to compensate for fluctuations in private investment and to maintain full employment.
In the past the government has replied, when these proposals were brought to its attention, that they could not be proceeded with until the taxation agreements were generally accepted. Now, there is only one province remaining without a tax rental agreement, and there is surely no longer any excuse for delaying the implementation of its own proposals made to the provinces in 1945. Incidentally, these proposals followed a long series of discussions, all of which are outlined for those who would read in the voluminous reports of the Rowell-Sirois commission, reports which, when they were presented, we believed would form the basis for better relationships and found better conditions for, not only the provinces but for all the people of Canada who live in the various provinces.
And this reminds me of at least one other respect in which the federal government is to blame for this new issue between the premier of Quebec and the federal parliament. Since 1950 meetings between representatives of the federal and provincial governments on matters connected with tax rental agreements have been adjourned, or as I recollect, on the understanding that there would be a permanent committee under the chairmanship of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson).
