speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I imagine hon. members will understand if I fail to take time today to give consideration to the amendment and subamendment which have been moved this afternoon. The amendment itself is long and involved, and I should like to have time to give it consideration. I would also like to take plenty of time to give consideration to the way in which the amendment has been modified as the result of the subamendment just moved by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell).
The leaders of the smaller groups on this side of the house, as was just said, do not have unlimited time and for that reason we have to be more selective in the things about which we speak in the budget debate. If I do fail this afternoon to mention any of these which are considered to be of first-line importance it will not be because I do not attach importance to them, but simply because I have not time to deal with them and other things as well. However, there will be several speakers in the debate from our group, and we shall try to deal with all of these things that touch the lives of the people in the country, and upon which it will be necessary for us to make a pronouncement.
My hon. friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), has presented what he says is his last budget. Such an occasion calls for some things to be said that might not be said in the course of an ordinary budget debate. The minister's qualities, his affability, his engaging personality, his cordiality at all times have won for him I think a sure place in the affection of hon. members and of the people of Canada. So long as budgets of this kind are going to be presented to parliament, there is no one I would rather see present them. May I add that no one but the Minister of Finance could get away with such a budget as this one with less resistance.
The high regard that I have for the minister but sharpened the keen regret that I felt on Tuesday evening last as he made his presentation in his usually effective way and very jaunty style, that provision after provision of his budget made it clear to me that 83276-253J
The Budget-Mr. Low he missed a golden opportunity to present a budget which would have been a departure from the ball and chain budgets of the past, because that is what they have been; and especially is it a matter of regret at this hour when the scourge of unemployment has again descended on Canada, and has already taken heavy toll in too many of our Canadian communities. This is an hour in Canadian history when even though they are employed the breadwinners in so many homes are experiencing hardship and privation and are having a very difficult time to make their take-home pay cover bloated costs and overgrown living expenses. At this hour, the minister could have brought down a budget that could have dispelled the ugly threat and at the same time made possible a decent standard of living in every Canadian home.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the message of his budget could have been a ringing assurance to the people of Canada that the maintenance of that decent standard of living that I just mentioned would be secure. If that had been the case, the minister's last budget would have been an historic one and would have brought him fame and the abiding satisfaction that always comes to one when he renders a real service to the millions of his fellow citizens. Instead of a message of real assurance and hope, what did the minister give to the people last Tuesday? Well, clearly his message was this: "If you have tears, prepare to shed them now. But if weeping over my nine previous budgets has drained you of tears, I have arranged to lower the tariffs on tear gas to help you find some tears of crocodile size for this, my tenth effort. My generosity, fellow Canadians, overcomes me. Come, let us weep together." That is just about the message of last Tuesday's budget.
I say this with deep regret: The minister, unless he is ready at the eleventh hour to accept the suggestions of changes, has missed his great opportunity in the same way as the Hon. Mr. Dunning missed a similar opportunity under similar although more pronounced circumstances in 1929 and again in 1936, and as the Hon. Mr. Bennett did in 1931.
Hansard records a famous speech made in this house many years ago by an illustrious Canadian, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. On this particular occasion Sir Wilfrid Laurier indulged in this effective oratorical declaration: "Canada needs three things:	The first is
transportation; the second is transportation; and the third is transportation." Transportation was Canada's greatest need in Sir Wilfrid Laurier's day. We have made progress since

The Budget-Mr. Low then in providing this country with transportation, although I feel sure that if Sir Wilfrid had been at the helm between the two wars and since world war II especially, the trans-Canada highway would long ago have been completed. We do not need transportation so badly as we did in his day, but we still need transportation in some parts of the country. But if Sir Wilfrid Laurier were here today he probably would say, to meet the challenge of this hour: "Canada needs three things: The first is markets; the second is markets and the third is markets."
Our home market is the best market we have. It could be a much better one, much better than it is if we followed the right financial and budgetary principles to make it so. For the optimum development of that home market we do need transportation of a form, not the kind of transportation about which Sir Wilfrid Laurier spoke but the widespread distribution amongst the Canadian people of that medium which transports goods over the counter from the merchants' shelves to the consumers who need and want them; or, in the case of durable goods, from the warehouses to the farms or the factory. What Canada needs most right now is a home market well supplied with a properly adjusted, continuous flow of purchasing power that will permit our people to buy and use all they want of what we can and do produce.
The government claims that we have prosperity in Canada, and it claims credit for bringing that prosperity. I spoke a moment ago about Sir Wilfrid Laurier, but he described in his speeches a potential prosperity for Canada by reference to vast undeveloped resources, as they were then. Well, these still exist in spectacular abundance in Canada. We have today a tremendous flow of goods and services provided by the developed resources of this nation. Those goods are in the form of food, clothing and articles that are useful, and they take the drudgery out of life in the home and on the farm; services such as electricity, transportation, hospitalization and so on exist, and these can be made to exist in ever-increasing quantities at levels sufficient to bring a great degree of comfort to every last citizen in our country. But, Mr. Speaker, so many thousands of our own people are not enjoying that prosperity for the simple reason that it has not been brought within their reach through wise financial, economic and monetary means.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the statesman about whom I was just speaking, said at one time: "I will give you a prosperity you can feel in your pockets." Mr. Speaker, Canada needs that kind of prosperity in this hour, and needs it desperately.
IMr. Low.]

the kind of budget he did. It may be too late for the minister to do so, but he should still imagine himself in the position of the head of a family, and without a job and take-home pay.
For that reason I would like to quote a letter which appeared in the February 22 issue of the Toronto Globe and Mail. I have no hesitation, Mr. Speaker, in quoting this because it is short and because it was written by a responsible secretary of an association of social workers who get right down among the people and see them in their homes. This is the letter, and I quote:
The executive committee of the Canadian Association of Social Workers, representing over 400 men and women giving service to families and children through various social welfare organizations in greater Toronto, is deeply concerned about the situation facing many families whose breadwinner is now unemployed and for whom there are no unemployment benefits or whose period of benefit has expired.
At the present time there is no assistance available from any official source for such families, the city of Toronto having provision only for unemployables and federal and provincial authorities not having organized in any way to meet this widespread need.
Last year, after more careful study by the Canadian Welfare Council and its membership across Canada, representations were made to the government at Ottawa and to all provincial governments regarding the urgent necessity of having some overall and permanent provision made to meet the situation and avoid the destitution and disruption of normal family living which today faces many families through no fault of their own. As far as can be observed, nothing has been done to make effective the recommendations made in this report or to evolve any satisfactory alternatives. Unemployment of able-bodied employable people who need and want work is a national problem which strikes at the very roots of family life and causes untold suffering.
We feel that all citizens should be fully aware of this situation and should do all in their power to urge upon the federal and provincial governments to appropriate funds for the suitable relieving of need, and upon the municipal government to extend its relief program pending the availability of government resources for this purpose.
Many people today in Toronto are actually suffering from hunger because of unemployment due not only to seasonal interruptions but to closing down or reduction in many industries.
The letter is signed by Miss Betty Quiggin, corresponding secretary of the association which I have named. What Miss Quiggin reports about Toronto has undoubtedly been true of many other Canadian cities for quite a number of months now.
With that picture in mind let me refer to an incident which involved one of the most capable and intelligent ministers of this government. In the Globe and Mail of February 11 last there appears a report of what took place when a labour deputation came to Ottawa and made six recommendations to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). The minister at that time insisted

that the backlog of demand for farm implements had been filled, and therefore the production of them must be reduced; and that members of the labour unions involved must seek other jobs.
Now, listen to this, and I quote from the Globe and Mail report of February 11 last:
The brief, which was a joint presentation of the United Auto Workers Union and the United Steel Workers, both C.C.L.-C.I.O. affiliates, said it was incorrect to state that the decline resulted from farmers being adequately supplied with implements. The 1951 census revealed that for every 100 farms in Canada, there were only 64 tractors, 53 passenger cars, 31 trucks, 29 gasoline engines and 32 electric motors. The problem, said the brief, was that many farmers were financially unable to buy equipment.
I think it must be abundantly clear that the real answer is to be found in that quotation from the article in the Globe and Mail. That article reveals the answer to the question of how to solve the problem of the hour, not only for the farm implement industry, but the whole unsolved problem of distribution in a situation where the problem of production has been completely solved. The answer is simply: Make the consumer or user financially able to buy, and he will do the job of keeping our economy in balance and unemployment at the irreducible minimum. That is the solution and the only effective solution.
That news item to which I referred gave the capable and intelligent Minister of Trade and Commerce credit for this statement:
It was no longer the case that everything and anything produced could be sold.
In that single sentence the Minister of Trade and Commerce put his finger on the frame of mind which is responsible for the iniquities in this budget and which have been in every budget presented to this house since 1929. Not only the iniquities it contains but the benevolences which it also contains. Any useful and every useful thing which can be produced could be sold. The only reason they are not all sold is that those who need and want them have not the money with which to buy them. The medium which transports them over the counter or out of the warehouse is not available to so many of the people of this country so that they cannot make use of these things which are produced for them.
In the commercial letter put out by the Canadian Bank of Commerce dated February 19, 1954, there is to be found this short but potent paragraph:
The task ahead, and this applies to every segment of the economy, is to maintain economic activity at current levels. Above all else, it would seem essential, in this regard, that increasing attention be given to the consumption side of the equation.
The Budget-Mr. Low
There, Mr. Speaker, you have it in a nutshell from a bank which is doing big business in this country and which has its finger on the pulse of the economic situation. The problem before us, therefore, seems to be as clear as day. Now, if ever, business must be kept steady and as free as possible from heavy jumps and declines. Certainly we would be utterly stupid to allow a depression to come upon us, or even a serious recession. I remind hon. members that our enemies will be impressed with our economic strength and the well-being of our people just as much as they will be impressed by our defensive military strength. They will become proportionately more bold and determined if they see unemployment grow or even continue at the level which has existed in this country over the past several months.
From the minister's speech of last Tuesday I note that he forecasts an upturn in the last six months of 1954 in Canada. He bases his hopes, to some degree at least, upon the improved situation in the United States. At least, he mentioned that as one of the reasons that he had for the forecast. As a consequence of his faith in the future, the minister in this present budget made very infinitesimal provision to take care of the present situation. I must be extremely critical of the failure of the government to take action on unemployment, not only just now but weeks ago when it became apparent that it was growing beyond the seasonal limit.
I think that the minister and the government are to be criticized for taking the position that simply because there appears to be some chance of a favourable upturn in the economic situation in the United States, our own trends will follow suit later this year. It seems to me the minister fails to bear in mind that the favourable turn in the United States came about as a consequence of deliberate and well-planned governmental action. They did not stand pat in the hope that everything would turn out all right in their country. The government got busy and made tax concessions to the people. They prepared to spend more money, to make credit easier to the public, to push housing and a number of other things deliberately chosen to stimulate employment and to keep activity at a healthy level. But, by contrast, the government of Canada decided to stand pat and to let things take their own sweet course back to something like a favourable level.
Let us just suppose for one moment that the minister's hopes for the last six months of 1954 do not materialize. Then what? That is the question. Certainly it is clear that this
4004	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Low budget makes no provision whatsoever to meet such a situation as that; not for a moment. This budget is definitely not the kind of budget that Canada needs at the present time. I say that the provisions of this budget would be woefully inadequate to meet the situation in Canada at the end of the first six months of this year if the expected upturn does not materialize.
The minister in his budget should have provided for whatever eventuality might arise later in this year, particularly in view of the facts as they are at the present time. The budget that we are now considering should have 'been one which provided for quick encouragement of increased consumer purchases. It should have been one providing for encouragement of increased production in many lines in order to keep up employment. It should have been one to provide for the use of a money mechanism which would get purchasing power into the hands of the ultimate consumers quickly and directly so that, by their effective demand, they could bring and keep the balance at or near the point of equilibrium.
More specifically, Mr. Speaker, this budget should have provided for a much greater reduction of taxation than it provides for. We are all grateful, of course, for the small things which the Minister of Finance did for the people by way of tax relief but I feel, as does my friend the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar, that in so much of the field that was covered by the very small reductions which the minister brought in the ultimate consumer will not feel the effects. He is the one who needs the help in this country. He is the only one who can correct the situation by his effective demand.
The municipalities are going to feel happy about the removal of the sales tax on roadbuilding equipment, but I am going to say this: The school divisions and districts of this country will not share that happiness because the same tax was not removed from their purchases of school buses to carry the children to school. They look upon the sale tax on buses as a means used by the federal government to make the school districts collectors of taxes for them from the farmers and other ratepayers in the districts, as it really is. It is simply a method used by the federal government to have the school districts collect for the federal government taxes that the average ratepayer in the school districts does not understand and cannot see.
Canadian housewives, of course, will be thankful for the removal of the excise tax on some items and its reduction on others; but they will never reconcile themselves to 

a situation where they have to pay a very substantial price differential over what their opposite numbers pay for the same thing down across the line in the United States. One could refer to cottons, electrical goods, dress goods and so on. Another good example is this. An American can buy a Chevrolet standard model automobile just across the line from Oshawa for from $500 to $700 less than Canadians can buy the same car. On the purchase of such an automobile in Canada the purchaser pays to the federal government over $500 in sales and excise taxes alone. We impose a 10 per cent sales tax and a 15 per cent excise tax at the manufacturer's level, but the United States has had the good sense to refrain from that practice over the years.
The price differential between Canada and the United States on many items our people want to buy is striking. Cottons, electrical goods-which I have already mentioned- heavy hardware and automobiles are just a few examples. The differential has arisen quite largely as a result of the difference in taxation on commodities between the two countries. The result is that many thousands of Canadians who can afford to do so have been making regular shopping tours into the United States in order to bring back their legal quota of tariff-free purchases. I wonder whether the minister has ever thought of this fact: If just half of Canada's population were to spend only half of their customs-free allowance in the United States each year, $1,200 million of Canadian money would be spent across the line each year for things that are lower in price there than they are here. That is just another reason why the price differential should not be allowed to become great enough to encourage mass movement on shopping tours down into the United States. Imagine what $1,200 million extra spent in Canada would do for business and employment in this country!
The minister should have announced in this budget the abolition of that part of the sales tax which is not earmarked for old age pensions or, in the alternative, should have provided himself with the authority to abolish it if the expected upturn in economic activity and outlook does not materialize during the last six months of this year.
The sales tax imposed at the manufacturers level is a pyramiding tax, very largely responsible for many of the heavy price differences between Canada and the United States. It is the poor man's income tax. It puts some Canadian producers into a handicapped competitive position as far as trade is concerned and helps to clutter up trade.

For these and many other reasons which I could offer but which I have not time to deal with today, I say the sales tax should be abolished. This was the budget that should have provided for its abolition. This is a time of readjustment when many businesses are at or near the boom peak. To make the adjustments that are necessary, prices have got to come down enough to put Canadian businesses into a position to compete in a world of trade where competition has again become very keen.
Tax reductions of the magnitude I have suggested would stimulate industrial activity and reduce unemployment. Moreover, while the minister fears that he would not be able to replace the lost revenue I am convinced that by reducing the tax burden as I have suggested he would bring down prices in Canada. With lower prices, our people would buy more, and so stimulate business from the retail level on back to the primary producer. More people would be put to work and unemployment would cease to bedevil many parts of Canada. Not only that, but I say that the minister's tax base would also be preserved so that his actual loss of revenue would be small, if any.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, as I see that my time is about up, may I say this. Coupled with the type of tax reductions that I have suggested, the present and foreseeable future situation calls for an all-out housing drive. What I say is that you are not going to be successful in that housing drive unless interest rates on long-term mortgage loans are brought somewhat lower, and unless money at quite low interest rates is made available to municipalities and limited dividend corporations for low income housing projects.
Every effort should be made to push the completion of the trans-Canada highway and to provide for federal participation in a highway system for Canada. Work on the St. Lawrence seaway and various developmental schemes should be pushed ahead as fast as possible.
Finally, the minister while this budget is before the house ought to provide himself with a monetary mechanism that will make it possible to inject purchasing power directly from its birthplace into the hands of ultimate consumers so that they can quickly convert it into effective demand, and thus exert a stimulating influence on declining business activity. The production is already in existence, and as much more as we want can be brought into existence. The need for old age pension increases, war veterans allowance increases, and blind pension adjustments is
The Budget-Mr. Houck very great. We have every material requirement to fill these needs and make these people in these brackets to which I have referred happy, except the financial means. We in this group strongly urge the use of the Bank of Canada to provide all the new money that is required at cost. This would be one step at least towards emancipating our people from the Frankenstein which we have allowed to grow up in our midst, and which threatens to destroy all freedom.
If we fail, Mr. Speaker, at this hour to provide the purchasing power to enable every Canadian to enjoy the material things our country is producing and can produce, we will be letting our people down and endangering the security of our country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As this is the first time I have availed myself of the opportunity to speak since becoming a member of this house, I should like to follow the time-honoured custom of congratulating the Speaker and you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, upon your appointments to these high offices. I am not saying it in a boastful attitude whatever, but I have had the privilege and honour of serving under quite a few Speakers in the Ontario legislature, and I should like to say to Mr. Speaker and to you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, that although many verbal bouquets have been thrown to both of you-yes, almost reaching the point of orchids-I want to say that you are by far the two best looking Speakers under whom I have ever had the privilege of serving.
When I first arrived in this house I felt rather at home because of the fact the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) served with me for some six or seven years in the Ontario legislature. I had the privilege also of sitting alongside the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll); the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Conacher) and the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel), so I really felt at home.
I have listened with a lot of amusement to the various speakers talking about then-various ridings. I presume that this debate, along with the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, does serve a useful purpose because of the fact a member has to say something about the importance of his riding. This afternoon I find myself in a rather peculiar position. I do not have to say anything about Niagara Falls. The whole world knows about Niagara Falls. I doubt if any city in Ontario or in the whole Dominion of Canada gets more free advertising over radio and television than does Niagara Falls. Yesterday afternoon I was rather interested in listening to Gracie Fields during her excellent program

The Budget-Mr. Houck on television refer to the fact that she had spent her honeymoon at Niagara Falls. That city is known as the outstanding honeymoon centre of the world, Mr. Speaker. Then, too, we have the rather doubtful honour that quite a few come back later on to commit suicide.
I do want to say that we in Niagara Falls are not jealous or selfish in any respect. We want to share it with the rest of the world. I am sure I could say to the hon. member for Spadina, whose home is in Toronto, that if he happened to be abroad in any foreign country and a small child came up to him and asked, "Where are you from?", when he replied "From Toronto", that child would immediately say "How far is that from Niagara Falls?", in order to know just where the hon. member did come from. In fact, we are so beautiful at Niagara Falls and so well known throughout the world that I had a dream the other night. My dream went something like this. I had gone up the steps to St. Peter, if a politician ever gets up the steps to St. Peter, and St. Peter said, "Where did you live?" I said, "Niagara Falls." He said, "That is a beautiful place, I do not think you are going to like it up here."
Speaking in a more serious vein, Mr. Speaker, we in Niagara Falls are exceptionally proud of our splendid relationships with our brothers and sisters directly across the Niagara river. I suggest that we provide a wonderful example to the rest of the world of those things called democracy or free enterprise. In the vicinity of the border line we do not merely give lip service to that thing we call democracy, but we actually live it. We have now lived for almost a hundred and forty years in peace and harmony with our good neighbours to the south of us. The rainbow arch, which is visible most of the day, is indeed a symbol of the peace and friendship between two great countries and two great friends.
I know that during the course of the next few weeks we are going to hear some criticisms of the budget. Perhaps some other remarks will be made from a jealous and selfish point of view, but I think all hon. members agree with me that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has brought down a very fine budget. I must say that we in Canada have been fortunate indeed, regardless of our political stripe, in having had very fine ministers of finance. I believe, however, that the name of our present minister, the Hon. Douglas Abbott, will go down in history as one of the finest ministers of finance we have ever been privileged to have.


There are a few comments I should like to make, pertaining to the St. Lawrence and to hydro, both of which are near and dear to my heart because I come from a hydro riding. I believe, Mr. Speaker, there are always occasions in one's life which stand out. One such occasion that I recall most vividly was nineteen years ago when I had the honour of moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne in the Ontario legislature. I am sure that my speech today will be another occasion that I shall remember for many years.
I should like to deal with a subject of great importance, not only to the welfare, economy and future prosperity of Ontario but to this great Dominion of Canada. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure it is shared by other hon. members, the signing of the agreement between the government of Ontario and the dominion government at Ottawa on December 3, 1951, marked an historic milestone in bringing the St. Lawrence seaway and power project closer to realization than it has been at any time in the long history of negotiations on this vital development. Under the terms of that agreement the Ontario government entered into a contract with the dominion government authorizing the Ontario government to develop the Canadian power rights of the international section of the St. Lawrence river with an appropriate authority in the United States.
Now, in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that agreement was not only historic but it was significant for a number of reasons. First of all it revealed very clearly that the St. Lawrence seaway and power project is an undertaking which men of action, regardless of their political views, recognize as being vital to the future progress of Ontario and Canada and of fundamental importance to the welfare of the people of this province and to the Canadian people in general. The St. Lawrence project is therefore one which transcends political considerations. It points up the fact that the public men who have been working untiringly to make it a reality are Canadians first, regardless of their political affiliations.
The subject of harnessing the power of the St. Lawrence has been the subject of negotiation between Canada, Ontario, the United States and the state of New York for over half a century. To the average citizen of Ontario and Canada the St. Lawrence power project is a mammoth undertaking that has seemed to appear and disappear from our field of notice always without finality one way or another.

Representing as I do the Niagara Falls district of the province of Ontario I have always been intensely interested in the development of hydroelectric power and in the power needs of our communities. One has only to recall that a little less than thirty years ago the average household in the province of Ontario was using only half a horsepower for lighting and one-and-a-half horsepower for electrical appliances. Today the connected load is more likely to be more than two horsepower for lighting and between twelve and fourteen horsepower for appliances.
This increase, coupled with the tremendous building program and industrial expansion, makes us realize that unless something is done to maintain the supply of low-cost power Ontario will face a critical situation in the near future. And I know that the most immediate and the most important concern of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of the province has always been with the shortage of power, not with the surplus of power as some people are led to believe.
Every citizen of the province of Ontario therefore should have a deep interest in the situation governing the St. Lawrence power project. Many of us thought that the negotiations for the St. Lawrence had possibly terminated with the great lakes-St. Lawrence development basin agreement in 1941. Events have proved how we were wrong. Canada waited eleven years for the United States to ratify that agreement. Finally our government decided that the 1941 agreement was superseded by the international joint commission order of October 29, 1952. This ruling gave approval to the Canadian and United States applications for the joint development of the power project on the St. Lawrence river, and led the way to the possibility of an all-Canadian seaway.
And I think it is a matter of interest to us members of the house to know that Canada has already spent some $300 million on various sections of the St. Lawrence, compared with the United States expenditure of approximately $93 million. And according to the Department of Transport, fifty per cent of Canada's expenditures were made during the period when each construction dollar represented something like four of today's dollars.
It is therefore reasonable to assume that the cost to Canada to the present day has been something like a billion dollars. The seaway is of course of tremendous importance to Canada and, despite the fact that the major portion will be located in Ontario, the far-reaching effect on our economy makes it of prime importance to every province in this great dominion.
The Budget-Mr. Houck
And, important as the seaway may be, the power project is by far the matter of greater urgency, in fact a matter of immediate urgency, if the future of Ontario is to be protected. Ontario hydro electric officials have made this fact abundantly clear on many occasions. Since 1945 demands for power have increased at a rate which is without parallel in the history of our province. And when one realizes that more than half of Canada's industrial output stems from the province of Ontario, and that this province leads in agricultural production, it can be easily seen that the power project is also of vital importance to this dominion.
Ontario hydro has stated on many occasions that the power needs of the people of that province must be met if our present high standard of living and growing economy are to be maintained. In an effort to keep pace with the growing demand for power, hydro has utilized every major source of power within economic transmission distance of large load centres. Despite a tremendous construction program involving more than a billion dollars, Ontario hydro will still be faced with a shortage of power towards the end of this decade.
During the seven immediate post-war years industrial consumption of power increased by 45-7 per cent, commercial use of power increased by 132-5 per cent and domestic use was up by 145-8 per cent. Farm electrification has progressed at such a rapid pace that farmers in Ontario at the end of 1953 were using 272 per cent more power than in 1945. During this same period the number of rural customers increased by 215,295.
There can be little wonder that Ontario hydro is deeply concerned about the continued delay in getting action on the St. Lawrence. All thinking people realize that, as Canada's leading mining, manufacturing and agricultural province, Ontario must have a new large source of low-cost power in the next few years if it is to maintain its present phenomenal expansion.
The St. Lawrence is the only answer, apart from high-cost steam generated power or the development of small sites which at present would not be economical because of their remote location.
Ontario hydro is, of course, studying the feasibility of using atom power. But, unless the development of this new source is much more advanced than I am led to believe, we cannot expect low-cost power from atomic energy for many years to come or even if it does come.
Ontario hydro's program of power expansion will be completed in 1957. At that time its dependable resources will have been

The Budget-Mr. Houck increased by some 132 per cent, allowing for the fact that the United States may be, at this time, making full use of its allocated diversion of waters at Niagara. Even with this tremendous increase in resources it is obvious to the people of Ontario that the 1,100,000 horsepower to which Ontario is entitled from the St. Lawrence will be required by 1958 if the present rate of growth is to be maintained. In fact, I am informed that every one of the 6,300,000 kilowatt hours a year from the St. Lawrence could be utilized right now for the benefit of Ontario and Canada.
The total potential power between lake Superior and Montreal based on the average amount of water available is in excess of 14 million horsepower. This is almost as great as the total installed capacity of all the hydroelectric plants in Canada today. Of course, the development of the entire St. Lawrence power potential is not economical or practicable. It is believed, however, that a total installation close to 10 million horsepower would be justified.
Of this 10 million, some 5,400,000 horsepower would be at Niagara, 2,200,000 horsepower at the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence, 2,000,000 horsepower at Beauharnois, and 1,100,000 horsepower at Lachine, Quebec. From this total installation available on the Niagara and St. Lawrence rivers some 5,500,000 horsepower would be available to Canada.
On the St. Lawrence river itself, as the figures show, about 5,400,000 horsepower would appear to be economically justified at Lachine, Beauharnois and the international rapids section. Of this, 4,300,000 horsepower would be in Canada and 1,100,000 horsepower in the United States at the international section.
Now, Mr. Speaker, with regard to our own power load, about a third of these total resources have been developed, to date. We have on the Niagara river a 500,000 horsepower plant, which is called the Sir Adam Beck Niagara generating station No. 1, at Queenston. We have another 180,000 horsepower at the Ontario power plant in Niagara Falls; another 145,000 horsepower at the Toronto power plant, also in Niagara Falls, and another 100,000 horsepower at the Canadian Niagara station. Then, Mr. Speaker, we have 200,000 horsepower at DeCew falls, which is very close to St. Catharines. At Beauharnois and at the Cedars plants in Quebec, I believe approximately 1,200,000 horsepower has been developed. Rapidly approaching completion, of course-and I am happy to say this-is
	s I
the new Ontario plant at Niagara Falls, which will develop 1,828,000 horsepower.
It is a pity to me, Mr. Speaker, that those who take a narrow and selfish view and those who fear their interests may be adversely affected have been loud and persistent in their clamour against the St. Lawrence project. Large sums of money have been spent in promoting anti-St. Lawrence publicity. Fortunately much of this deceptive propaganda has collapsed when subjected to careful study.
It is somewhat ironical when one considers that almost every major newspaper or publication has commented during the last few years on the fact that the St. Lawrence is one of the most important developments of our age. Despite the tremendous support which this scheme has enjoyed, however, we are still awaiting authority to proceed.
There can be little doubt of the need for an early start on this project. During the post-war years in Ontario the increase in industrial use of electricity has been enormous. More than 600 factories, new to Ontario, have been established; technical processes have been developed; personnel has been trained, power equipment installed and a strong broad industrial base has been laid. On this broad base industry is capable of rapid expansion. I need hardly add that it would also be the arsenal from which our defence production materials could be drawn if necessary.
You may recall that a treaty was negotiated in 1950 between the Canadian government and that of the United States permitting a larger diversion of water for power at Niagara. The Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario-and I give them full credit, Mr. Speaker-lost no time in beginning a development which will eventually harness the falling waters of Niagara river to develop a further 1,828,000 horsepower.
Since I come from Niagara Falls, Mr. Speaker, naturally I have taken a keen interest in this project, and I want to say this to the credit of the Hydro Electric Power Commission. Although the United States and the state of New York have the right and the power to use the available water at Niagara falls, along with the Hydro Electric Power Commission, for the last two years they have not seen fit to take any of it. I throw my chest out and my shoulders back in justifiable pride that we here in Canada, and in Ontario, have gone ahead and set a picture and a pattern for the people of the United States, and we have shown them what we can do with regard to the water that is available at Niagara for power purposes.

They are fighting at the present time, and will continue to fight over there for many months to come, as to whether or not that power should be developed either by private enterprise or by public enterprise. But while they are going on with their arguments we are going ahead, and we shall have that development finished in a very short time.
The Sir Adam Beck generating station No. 2 is scheduled to open officially next August 8. Truly remarkable progress has been made since construction began in December 1950, just two months after the final ratification of the Niagara river diversion treaty. The new plant, named in honour of the man who is the father of hydro in Ontario, is just upstream from the No. 1 plant at Queenston, which was at one time the largest hydroelectric station in the world. This new plant, the new diversion, is spread across an eight-mile distance. The works of the Niagara project include tremendous engineering feats by Canadians on the staff of the Ontario hydro. Two intake structures for the tunnels are located two miles above the famous falls, near Chippawa; the twin 54-mile long tunnels with diameters of 51 feet are being constructed under the city of Niagara Falls; the 2i-mile open-cut canal is almost complete and the new powerhouse at Queenston, located six miles below the cataracts, is rapidly taking shape.
I want to say this, Mr. Speaker, we have had very many fine hydro engineers not only in the province of Ontario but in the Dominion of Canada as well. 1 think I can say without fear of contradiction that among the finest was Dr. Harry Acres. Dr. Hogg was another fine efficient hydro engineer. We also had Mr. Hearn, who is now the chief engineer of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of the province of Ontario, and Mr. Andrews of the Harry Acres Company at Niagara Falls. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I can paraphrase the advertising slogan of a famous automobile company, which goes something like this: "When better cars are made, so and so will make them". I want to say, Mr. Speaker, without fear of contradiction: When better hydro engineers are produced, the Niagara Falls area will produce them.
Will you call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the
adjournment for the dinner hour I was telling the house something about the mammoth new
The Budget-Mr. Houck hydro development at Niagara Falls and I was also speaking about the willingness of Ontario and New York to co-operate to undertake the power development on the St. Lawrence at a cost of something over $600 million. I firmly believe that the benefits to the province of Ontario, the state of New York and, indeed, Canada and the great republic of the United States of America, will outweigh the original cost. Looking ahead we must picture in our minds just what this new source of power will mean to our people, and especially what it will mean to industry. One engineer has estimated that the power going to waste in the international section of the St. Lawrence is equivalent to the energy that could be created by 28 million healthy workingmen every year.
Over the last few years a great deal has been said concerning the decentralization of industry. One cause for concern, especially in the maritime provinces, is that the seaway and the power project may have a strong centralizing influence. I believe this government recognizes the importance of carrying out, in so far as it is possible, an orderly and economic policy of decentralization of industry. We must not forget this policy and steps should be taken to see that it is followed in every possible field.
In considering this power project we must not lose sight of the old saying that "trade follows the flag". The modern adaptation of this saying is that "industry follows power". Ever since the industrial revolution it has been traditional that industry developed where there was an adequate supply of primary power. I believe it is part of our national responsibility that every power resource that can be developed must be developed, and that it is the prime responsibility of this government or any other government to do so.
Power resources are all a part of our great national heritage. They are all part of the vision of development that the fathers of confederation had, and unless we are prepared to see that every single natural resource in Canada is developed we are not going to meet that challenge and achieve the destiny envisioned by the pioneers, the fathers of confederation.
Almost all the opposition that the seaway project and the power development are meeting seems to come from extremely powerful lobbies in the United States, lobbies that seem to have bushels of money with which to operate and seem to be accomplishing what they have set out to do. It is my firm belief that much of the objection to these developments is coming from selfish business interests who care nothing about the country's

The Budget-Mr. Houck welfare as long as they are well looked after. Another thing that should stand out prominently in all these negotiations between Canada and the province of Ontario is that politics have played no part whatsoever. Probably no bigger football has ever existed n Washington than the St. Lawrence project tself.
I quite well recall that some ten or twelve years ago, when I had the privilege of serving on the Hydro Electric Power Commission of the province of Ontario, we at that time met the whole Senate committee from Washington for three days along the St. Lawrence. We inspected the whole project and at the end of the three days' conference they as much as assured us that the St. Lawrence project could be proceeded with within two months. That is twelve years ago.
In time of peace shortage of power is unfortunate. In the event of war a power shortage is a national disaster. As the best friend that the United States has among the nations, Canada is deserving of better treatment than she has had in relation to engagements for power developments on rivers in which both countries have a common interest. Canada's efforts to obtain the St. Lawrence projects have been backed by almost all representatives across the dominion. Without the wonderful co-operation shown between the two levels of government, federal and provincial, Canada's firm stand could not have been upheld. I think that our government leaders from Newfoundland to British Columbia are to be congratulated for the splendid spirit they have shown and the foresight they have had for the future of our great country.
I want to apologize to the house. I realize that I have probably spoken longer than I intended. I am also aware of the old saying that the brain can only absorb what the seat can endure, and I promise that I will only be another minute or two. I want to bring to the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) the fact that we are badly in need of the new Burlington bridge at Burlington. I hope that the same spirit of cooperation that has existed between the dominion and the province with respect to the St. Lawrence seaway will exist with regard to that bridge. On week days and holidays it takes you longer to travel through that strip at Burlington than it does to go from Niagara Falls to Burlington, a distance of some forty-five miles. The present bridge is one of the great handicaps that tourists meet in getting through the traffic hazard at Burlington.
I also want to draw to the minister's attention the bridge at Homer. The bridge is
TMr. Houck.]

raised when ships are passing through, and on many days last year I have seen the traffic lined up from the bridge in St. Catharines to the city of Niagara Falls, a distance of twelve miles, waiting for the bridge to be lowered.
I want to pay my respects to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) for the very fine officials they have at our border points, especially at the ports of Niagara Falls and Fort Erie. These customs and immigration officials are the first greeters of our immense tourist traffic, and very seldom are there complaints from tourists with respect to the treatment they receive from these splendid officials. Our first impressions are our lasting impressions, and many times tourists at Niagara Falls have told me of the wonderful way in which they were handled by these fine officials at the border. I say to the ministers concerned that they are to be congratulated on having such fine officials. They are doing a lot to sell this great Dominion of Canada.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that it is a distinct honour, one that I will cherish for many a day, that I should be the first representative of the new riding of Niagara Falls. I hope I may carry out my duties with honour and distinction to that great riding.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising tonight to take part in this budget debate may I say that in my opinion it is probably the most serious in all the years I have been here because in preceding years business was on the upswing. But now we have come to a period of readjustment and, as the minister pointed out in his presentation of the budget the other evening, business and industry have to sharpen their pencils and get down to brass tacks. My first reaction to the budget was that the the people had asked for bread and were given a stone.
On April 1 taxes went up in a sense. We had to pay more postage for first-class letters, and while on budget night a few crumbs of comfort were thrown in by the reduction of taxes on certain lines they amounted to so little that the resentment stirred up by the increase in postage rates was greater than the acclaim that greeted the minister's budget.
I criticize the budget on several grounds. It failed to take into consideration mounting unemployment. I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and other cabinet ministers have said that the condition is seasonal but it is hardly seasonal when unemployment is double what it was a year

ago. It was seasonal then. Therefore that is not quite the answer to the problem. I realize, Mr. Speaker, that you warned the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdon-nell) about reading quotations from newspapers. I do not intend to read a quotation, but I have here in my hand excerpts from many Canadian newspapers, all of which point to the serious problem confronting many areas of this country due to mounting unemployment.
One other point the minister failed to mention is that business failures have increased by 19 per cent from a year ago. That underlines how much tougher it is to do business today, and how competition from foreign countries is depriving many of our industries of their business, and the people who work in them of their livelihood. The source of my information in that regard is the dominion bureau of statistics publication, volume 32, No. 3, which deals with business failures and which states that such failures have increased by 19 per cent over the third quarter of 1952. That, in my opinion, is a fair barometer of what is going on in this country.
The minister also failed to take into consideration the shrinkage in freight tonnage or car loadings. That, to my mind, is one of the best indications of economic conditions as they exist today. A dominion bureau of statistics bulletin issued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce deals with this point. I have no wish to bore the house with an endless series of figures, but taking the month of October as a yardstick there were 825,607 tons less freight loaded in October 1952 compared with October 1951. Comparing the months of October 1951 and October 1953 there were 1,385,471 tons less freight loaded in 1953 than in 1951. That also is an indication of an economic trend within this country.
It occurs to me that possibly the next election is too far off to expect much in the way of tax reductions, but probably we will come back to that happy state of affairs as the years roll on. However, I wish to bring to the attention of the house some other factors which should be taken into consideration. Down through the years I have been here the government has effectively killed as far as was humanly possible every connection we have had with the British commonwealth and the United Kingdom, even to the extent of putting an eagle on the cap badge of the R.C.A.P. We have put all our trading goods in the United States basket, as it were, and this has resulted in the loss of our export markets. It has also resulted in a flood of United States goods into this country.

In accordance with your ruling, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to quote from a newspaper but I would like to refer to an item in the Windsor Daily Star of a week ago which pointed out that with respect to one item alone, namely onions, 243 carloads of United States onions were sold in 12 Canadian cities since January 1954. This took place while hundreds of thousands of bags of Canadian onions failed to find a market in the three southwestern counties of Ontario and in the Bradford marsh area, northwest of Toronto.
Is it any wonder then that implement companies and their employees are idle and farmers cannot buy their produce? It must be obvious that farmers are not going to turn around and buy the products of factories whether they produce textiles or farm implements.
However, I would like to reiterate that the government has severed as far as possible our British connections in terms of trade and in many other ways. The government has put its trust in the United States market, despite the fact that recent experiences indicate that we have been shut out of that market in terms of dairy products, oats, and rye, and this was done without any consultation with our government, regardless of the Geneva trade treaties to which we as well as they were signatories.
These Geneva trade treaties have cramped our field of action. We signed this treaty as did 33 other nations and attempted to bring about comparative tariffs, but we fail to take into consideration that many of these countries who are signatories to this treaty have a much lower standard of living and lower wage rates than we have. Despite that fact we are expected to compete with them.
I would like to draw to the attention of the house the plight of the electrical goods industry. The average wage rate in that industry today, both in the United States and Canada, is $1.67 an hour. The countries which supply electrical goods to this country, such as Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and other countries, have an average wage rate running from as high as 37 cents to as low as 27 cents. Is it any wonder therefore that we have men idle when these goods can be delivered at a price which is far below our cost of production? Regardless of this the minister tells industry and labour to sharpen their pencils and to become more efficient. The comparison I have given you as far as electrical goods are concerned applies equally well to the textile and other industries.
4012	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. H. O. White
I think I can agree with the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin) that optimism has its place, but so has a little realism, and I believe that realism was lacking in last week's budget speech.
Barring a miracle it is very likely that milk supplied to the milk concentrating factories of this country may slip down a few cents in price, and if the government wishes to bring on more unemployment all they have to do is to take the floor price from under farm products. They will then find even more industries laying off their workers.
While I am dealing with the farming industry and their problems I would like to say a word about daylight saving time. We have railway time, airline time, bus time, and daylight saving time. We will have city time and country time. If this government believes in democracy then they ought to have a referendum so that the people can decide whether we should or should not have daylight saving time. The whole problem is complex and extremely confusing. For example, in Windsor, Chatham, and western Ontario they have eastern standard time, while London and many other cities have daylight saving time. In my opinion those who wish to go to work an hour earlier should do so, but there is no reason to change the clocks.
A year or so ago, though it seems just like yesterday, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) returned from his tour of South America. I remember his telling us about the great opportunities there for expansion of trade; but from that day onward our trade with those countries has gone down and down. Maybe it is not his fault, but he certainly promised us some great things as far as those South American countries were concerned. I hope he does not take another jaunt around there to sell Canadian products and come back with the same results.
Taxation plays a bigger part in our economy than many of us realize. It is estimated that it requires an investment of between $8,000 and $10,000 to equip a factory so that it will employ one man and so on for every employee. In other words, the amount of money that is drawn off in taxation reduces the number of potential jobs in this country. On more than one occasion I have pointed out to the house and to the government that inflation is the root cause of many of our troubles. Through inflation we have priced ourselves out of world markets. Inflation is the most subtle and sinister invasion of the assets and wealth of the people. In Germany


this inflation ended in Hitler's dictatorship, because when you can control currency and destroy people's faith in their monetary system you can do with them almost anything that you desire to do.
From the budget speech I note that the government have finally adopted a suggestion of the Conservative party-and incidentally it is one of my own-that the sales tax on municipal purchases be done away with. I am glad to see the adoption of that suggestion.
I am coming back again, Mr. Speaker, to what the minister said about labour and industry becoming more efficient and his telling them to sharpen their pencils and cut their costs. The strange part about that matter was that the government themselves failed to do that. The biggest business in the country, they neither sharpen their pencils nor become more efficient. I think here is a case where the government could and should give a lead to industry and labour by showing that they themselves can follow their own advice; but apparently they either are unable or unwilling to reduce the cost of government.
I want to return for a moment to our unfavourable trade balances. I have here in my hand the monthly summary of foreign trade published under the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This monthly summary shows imports for consumption from all countries. To summarize it quickly for you, in the month of January, 1952, imports from foreign countries amounted to $307-1 million and in January, 1953, they amounted to $327-8 million; in other words, they were up $20 million. As to our exports to foreign countries, they were down from $324 [DOT] 1 million to $317-3 million in the same months. In the months for which I have the figures here, namely January, February, March, April, May, June, July and August, of 1953, only two show a favourable trade balance, those of June and August. In June there was a favourable trade balance of $9-7 million and in August one of $1-6 million. As to the other months the figures range all the way from minus $87 million to minus $47 million, minus $35 million and minus $6-6 million. In other words, we are employing people outside of Canada to make the things that could well be made by our idle people.
Then as to imports for consumption, in the month of August, 1952 we imported agricultural and vegetable products to the tune of $33 million worth. In July, 1953 we imported $42 million worth. In other words, some of these onions that I was talking about have been brought into the country while our own were wasted. As to fibres, textiles and other products, in the same months our imports

for consumption went up from $25 million to $31 million; iron products, imports went up from $97 million to $150 million; chemicals and allied products went up from $13 million to $18 million; non-metallic minerals and like products went up from $54 million to $64 million. In other words the totals for these main groups imported into this country went up $100 million in the year from August, 1952 to July, 1953.
I say again, is it any wonder that we have idle people? While I am mentioning to the minister the matter of sharpening his pencil and becoming more efficient at home, may I say this. From the dominion bureau of statistics report I notice that the number of employees of the dominion government increased by 11,678 in the past twelve months.
There is another matter in the budget to which I want to draw the attention of the minister and the house. I refer to the matter of dominion-provincial relations. It is quite apparent to me-at least, it is my opinion- that that matter was dragged in as a red herring to draw the people's attention away from the serious economic and unemployment situation prevailing and away from the burdensome amount of taxation they are paying, amounting to something over $1,300 for a family of four in Canada before they have a dollar with which to buy their groceries, pay their rent or clothe themselves.
I would point out to the minister that over the years the Liberals too have had some resolutions in their platform. One was the health insurance plan which has been forecast every election year since 1919, but nothing has been done about it. They have promised to reform the Senate ever since 1867. But worst of all, they have failed to formulate plans to aid in the development of the natural resources of the country, thereby increasing employment in the country.
I want to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck) who preceded me. I was glad to note that he had at last become a disciple of that great man-probably the greatest of all Ontario citizens-Sir Adam Beck. I noticed that in his speech he also failed to mention the repudiation of the hydro contracts carried out under Mitchell Hepburn.
