speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the present budget now before us the government proposes to raise, including the special old age security tax, the sum of $4,765 million. Of that sum they propose to spend something over $2 billion on national defence. Because our national defence expenditures will take approximately 42 per cent of our total budget and because I did
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy not take part in the external affairs debate, I propose to deal with some aspects of our responsibility as a nation for helping to safeguard the survival of democracy and for making it work in the kind of world in which we live today.
The democratic world has, in our generation, fought two world wars to secure the survival of democracy against the onslaughts of nazi and fascist dictators. Today we are confronted with the problem of securing the survival of democracy against the advancing and ever-increasing forces of communist dictatorship. I believe we all agree this dictatorship is a much more sinister force than that which we fought in world war I and world war II. It is more sinister and more dangerous because, whereas the nazi and fascist dictators appealed chiefly to the racial superiority of one or two races, communist dictators appeal to the hungry and dispossessed peoples of every race everywhere.
We sometimes think today in terms of two worlds, communists and non-communists. The world in which we live is torn by tension between those two forces, between the two great most powerful states, Russia and the United States of America. In addition to that we are living today in an age of revolution. The world in which we live is, in my opinion, passing through the greatest revolution in its history. We are living in a world in which two-thirds of its population is rising up against inequalities of race and inequalities of economic opportunity.
We on this continent are inclined to think our great task today is to stop communism. We are sometimes inclined to believe that but for Russia we could all enjoy a stable peace. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we are experiencing today a world revolution for equality. I suggest, further, that were every communist in the world removed that revolution for equality would continue. Let us take a brief look at that world. We are told that there are 200,000 babies born into this world every day. Only one in three is white. Two of every three are born either in countries that have revolted and thrown out the white folk who govern them or in countries who are still trying to throw out the white folk. Only one in four of those babies is born a Christian. One in four is born in China. One in nine is born in India. Those born in India have a one to four chance of surviving infancy. Those who survive infancy have only a fifty-fifty chance of ever reaching maturity.
Half of those 200,000 babies born every day in this world, unless we can make

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy democracy work in other countries, will always be hungry. Many thousands of them will die of famine before reaching maturity. We are told today that two-fifths of the world's population can neither read nor write. Only five in every hundred in Africa, still a part of the free world, can read. Two billion of these sick, hungry, and illiterate people live in the free world, in that free world which we are trying to lead in a crusade against communism.
When we look at Russia, we think in terms of tyranny. When these millions in Africa, Asia, or South America look at Russia, tyranny does not frighten them. They have never known anything else. What they see is not tyranny but the possibility of liberation from landlords and local money lenders to whom they have been in debt all their lives and to whom they pay from 30 per cent to 100 per cent interest. They see not tyranny in Russia but the possibility of planned reconstruction of their country on the basis of modern machinery. They see possibly an end to all the misery and despair that is unknown to us, and such as we can scarcely imagine.
It is true that such sickness, hunger and misery is not anything new to these people, but this is the first time in their history that hundreds of millions have learned that because of new scientific knowledge, new technical skills, their suffering is unnecessary. They have now come to realize something they have never known before. There is plenty of evidence the peoples of Asia, Africa and South America are determined to solve their economic problems. The great question that confronts us as a member of the free world is whether or not we can demonstrate to these millions, in time, that democracy can offer them a better solution to their problems than can dictatorship.
I submit that it is only by doing that we can ever hope to hold these two billion people within the free world. In other words, unless we want to live in the communist dominated world, unless we are prepared to see communism dominating the world in which we live, we must make democracy work not only in our own countries, but in Asia, Africa and South America. We ask what we are doing in that regard. What are we doing to demonstrate to these people that democracy does offer them and can provide them with more freedom and security both in the field of economics and politics, than can communism.
Quite frankly I think we have made a fair beginning, though I admit it is but a beginning. If we compare the course of action


that was adopted by the victors of world war II with the course of action that was followed by the same victors of world war I,
I think we realize that we have been making some progress in this job of making democracy work. We have been making democracy work better in the domestic field in Great Britain, Europe and North America, and to some extent in the international field.
Before world war II one of our most painful social problems was that of mass unemployment, the inability of our economic system to employ a large sector of the available labour force in productive enterprise. Somehow we have managed to avoid mass unemployment since world war II. Some say that is because of our rearmament program, but I think an impartial observer must admit that our employment figures were nearly as high in 1948, 1949 and 1950, before we embarked upon our rearmament program, as they have been since that time. That is particularly true in this country.
To be quite frank I suppose we must admit that our rearmament program has been one factor in our provision for unemployment. To be frank again, we must admit that the scarcities created by the ravages of war in Europe have contributed markets for our products and enabled us to maintain a high degree of employment.
However unemployment is again raising its head in this country. And whether the government believes that that unemployment is seasonal or temporary, it is a factor involving half a million Canadians. The fact remains that even with our experience of the thirties we have not yet learned to provide full employment for all our people without recourse to rearmament or recourse to war, or depending upon shortages created by war.
That is one of the lessons which somehow we must learn in this and other countries of the free world, if we are to enable democracy to survive and if we are to prove to our own people and others the advantages of democracy over communism. If we turn again to the pre-war world we find that another of our difficulties was the inability to find employment for available savings and capital. Today on the other hand there is always a shortage of capital for investment in the numerous enterprises sponsored by government agencies and private firms within the free world system.
The third symptom of our domestic economy in the pre-war days, particularly in North America and Europe, was the stagnation of agriculture. Lack of markets made it necessary for us on this continent to burn food, to burn agricultural products we were

unable to dispose of. Today we are experiencing a veritable agricultural revolution in the mechanization of agricultural processes and in boosting agricultural output. We are getting nearer to the goal of being able to feed some of the hungry millions of the world than we were in the post-war years. There, again, we find today our granaries filled, bulging with wheat; we find ourselves without markets and unable to dispose of our wheat, while millions of people are hungry.
There again we must learn somehow to find a way of distributing food we can produce among the hungry peoples of the world. This buoyancy of our post-war economic system has been brought about, in part, by reason of war and rearmament, in part by shortages created by war and also in part by the shift of political power and influence within the countries of Europe and North America.
Since the war, under the pressure of public opinion, governments have been forced to devote a higher percentage of their production and net income to improving the standard of living of the common people within their borders. This has been made possible by a redistribution of our national income. Governments in every country enjoying representative forms of government, or government responsible to the electors, since the war have been taking bigger slices of the national income and redistributing it through welfare-state measures such as children's allowances, old age pensions, health insurance, workmen's compensation and the like.
That, and the increasing amount of capital investment made by governments or in government-sponsored or government-supervised and, in some cases, government-owned enterprises, have served to provide the consuming public with more spending power, and have served to remove the unbalance between classes in our domestic economy.
Here I think we need to stop before we take too seriously the advice of those who tell us that, because industrial workers have been receiving higher wages and because farmers have been receiving higher prices for their products, we are pricing ourselves out of world markets, and consequently the thing to do to regain those world markets is to begin reducing wages and farm prices. 1 think we would do well to stop and consider before we follow any such advice as that.
After all, we cannot maintain full production unless our consuming public have the wherewithal to buy that production. It is true that we must of necessity export a great part of our production, but we must take in turn from those countries to which we export goods of that country's origin. We must take these goods in exchange for ours. These
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy goods that we take back in exchange must in the final analysis be sold to our own people. Therefore, unless we can maintain in one way of another the purchasing power of our consuming public in Canada we have no hope of continuing the kind of prosperity we have enjoyed in the past.
Let us turn now to the international field where the unbalance between the nations that have and the nations that have not still remains to be adjusted. What have we done in that field? Again 1 say we have made a beginning, but nothing more than a mere beginning. Prior to world war II the only means by which the increasing capital of industrial metropolises could be spread throughout the world was that of foreign investment on private account and for profit. As masses of capital accumulated in one or two of the most advanced nations, it was lent to or directly invested in the less developed parts of the world. This method of investment led to the extension of actual sovereignty of the capital exporting nations over those in which the capital was invested. The necessity of providing some security for investments resulted in the whole world becoming colonized. It was this method which led to the partitioning and repartitioning of the globe and led to the frightful collisions between major industrial nations, the relations which we know as world war I and world war II.
That picture has changed somewhat since world war II. The whole mental climate of our times is inimical to that type of enterprise today. After world war II the economies of Britain, France, Germany, the rest of western Europe and Japan were shattered. In the past this problem would have been met as after world war I by raising of ordinary commercial loans from private investors in the United States. These loans would have been made with an eye to private profit. This time, after world war II, no one even supposed that this method could possibly be followed.
The economies of Britain, France, Germany and Japan have been largely restored through Marshall aid and similar arrangements. Much of the needed capital was exported as a free gift. Some of it was advanced on easy terms and modest interest rates. The capital was not raised voluntarily, but was provided by the United States government out of taxation compulsorily levied on the United States public. Whatever we may say about the United States' motives for this, the fact is that an entirely new way was found of rectifying to some extent the unbalance between the United States and Europe after the war.

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy
The real and gigantic job that now lies ahead of us in order to make democracy work and thereby save for the free world two billion people living in Asia, Africa and South America from going communist is to find some way whereby the United States, together with Canada, Great Britain and those European countries which are again going concerns, can pour their capital into Asia, Africa and South America. From China to Peru the majority of the human race remains untouched by the industrial revolution. Psychologically and politically they are waking up, and unless some acceptable means can be found of providing capital and technical knowledge to enable them to develop their countries they will certainly be lost to the free world. They will pass into the Russian orbit which can do far less for them economically than can democracy, but which will do even that little for them at the expense of those freedoms that we in the free world cherish.
In this field I submit we have fallen down badly so far. We have laid the foundation. We have the Colombo plan and the technical assistance plan within the United Nations; but to date work in this field has received very scant consideration. Our main efforts have been devoted to rearmament. We in Canada spent approximately $1 on economic aid for every $100 we spent on rearmament. Altogether we have been spending in Canada approximately $29 million a year on Colombo, economic aid and all the United Nations' agencies combined. That, I submit, is not good enough and is simply an indication of the fact that we do not realize in this country, nor do our allies in other countries realize, the magnitude of the greatest problem that confronts us today.
World war II, it is said, cost the United States $330 billion. If world war III began tomorrow, whether it began in Indo-China or wherever it began, the United States, Great Britain, Canada and other countries of the free world would immediately find the hundreds of billions of dollars needed to prosecute that war, but those same nations today can find a matter of millions instead of billions for the greatest of all tasks that now confronts the free world if we are to make democracy work. If, indeed, we are to enable democracy to survive.
Because of the immediate situation in regard to Indo-China, Mr. Speaker, we are in danger at this time of diverting our thought from the greater, the more important and long-term program of assisting the hungry and dispossessed peoples of the world. Whatever we may do, or whatever happens in Indo-China, we must not lose sight of the

fact that we must somehow, by some means, convince the leaders of the two billion not yet brought within the Russian orbit that democracy has more to offer them both in economic and political freedom and security than has communism.
Have we any reason whatever to believe that if the United States and other free nations choose to fight it out to the bitter end with the communists in Indo-China that China and other communist countries will not give assistance to the communists as they did in Korea? Surely, Mr. Speaker, with our experience in Korea, and the knowledge we now have of the powers of the hydrogen bomb, it is the part of sanity to try, as our own Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) suggested to us in his speech, by every means possible to secure a negotiated settlement of the dispute in Indo-China without embarking on another Korea. Such embarkation might very easily result in the use of the H-bomb by one side or by both.
Any move that will lessen the possibility of such a negotiated settlement will shock the conscience of the entire world today, and history may well regard the perpetrator of such a move as an enemy and not a friend of mankind. The United States and her allies in the free world may have to make some concessions to communist countries to achieve that kind of settlement in Indo-China. It may be possible that we may have to recognize Red China or admit Red China to the United Nations or open up avenues of trade with countries behind the iron curtain. We may have to make concessions to public opinion in France regarding the rearming of Germany. But none of these concessions will be half as terrifying to mankind as the possibility of the two great world forces using H-bombs against each other.
While on the subject of H-bombs, I want to say that in my opinion Canada's role should consist of using every possible effort to secure international agreement on two points; one, that there be no more trial explosions of H-bombs in the Pacific and, two, that this infernal machine, capable only of destruction, be outlawed from the face of the earth. The H-bomb just has no place in a world of human beings who still have some interest in survival.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate in its early stages, I wish at the outset to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) upon his budget and the message of assurance which it contains for the Canadian people. In the welter of pessimism that is being generated in Canada today, it is refreshing to have the chief financial officer

of the country paint an optimistic picture, a picture which, I think, is justified and supported by an economic review of last year's achievements and by an assessment of the critical economic factors that will affect the development of the country in the year ahead. If there is any relationship between the economic development of the country and the financial or economic policies pursued by its government-and that proposition has been widely urged in the house since the debate began-then I think the Minister of Finance should receive the commendation of the Canadian people for having presided over the financial affairs of the country in the period of its unprecedented economic growth.
In announcing another surplus the minister has continued his policy of adjusting the budget accounts to the state of the economy. It used to be a belief of public finance that a surplus was always desirable and that a deficit was always undesirable. But now-and this view has been presented only in recent times-it is true that a surplus or a deficit is neither necessarily good nor bad in itself, but derives its virtue from its accommodation to the need of the economy. Of recent origin also is the belief that the budget can be used as a defensive and offensive weapon in maintaining balance in the economy. Therefore, the government has continued its policy of creating surpluses in periods of prosperity for the prudent reason of retiring the public debt gradually but for the more solid reason of facing up to a deficit without extraordinary strain when such a policy is required in the national interest.
The gradual retirement of the public debt is useful because it reduces the annual burden of debt carrying charges and also because it appeases the distortion in income distribution which is inevitably associated with a large public debt. I believe that the Canadian public have supported this policy of creating surpluses. I believe an opposite policy would have bordered on imprudence, if not improvidence. Last year, the budget accounts reveal, Canada established new records in the gross national product, in employment and earnings, in the size of the labour force, in the rate of personal savings and in other categories of economic significance. The achievement of last year takes on additional perspective in view of the equal or greater achievement of previous years. The trend has been a steady and upward growth in the economy.
In view of this background one must ask himself whether the current unemployment problem represents a basic reversal in the upward growth of the Canadian economy. The minister faced this issue squarely and stated that the current unemployment is
The Budget-Mr. MacEachen the result of increased price competition from foreign suppliers and a general readjustment to a more competitive economy. If this diagnosis is correct, and no alternative diagnosis has yet been presented, then in my judgment the real solution does not lie within the realm of fiscal policy. By fiscal policy I mean the augmenting or enlarging of the stream of purchasing power through tax reductions or increased government expenditures. Such a measure at this time would not assist the specific industries facing price competition, because there is no presumption that consumers will buy higher-priced goods simply because purchasing power has been discharged into the economy.
Furthermore, the application of general fiscal measures would not likely have the desired effect unless there is a general malaise affecting investment, consumption, and government expenditures. No evidence has yet been brought forward to counteract the evidence of investment plans presented in the annual survey tabled in this house by the Department of Trade and Commerce. Defence expenditure will continue to play its role in sustaining the economy and the only sign of weakening among these three sensitive barometers is a weakening in purchasing power, and even with that weakening, purchasing power still remains strong.
If price competition from foreign markets is the problem then the short term solution is clear, if unacceptable. It lies in the realm of commercial policy. The quickest way to provide such price relief is through the application of a tariff against competing products. The minister has wisely resisted pressure for increased tariffs. Such a policy at this particular time would work against increased world production and against Canada's stake in multilateral trade.
I believe the high aspirations expressed by hon. members in the debate on external affairs have now taken practical effect, and this practical effect will be supported by the same firm purpose that was expressed in that debate. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, as a member for the province of Nova Scotia I can testify to the adverse internal effects further tariff increases might have on regions which must export their primary production.
It is my belief that Canada has reached the peak point in its unemployment and that the downward trend will soon be evident.
One phase of this problem which has been neglected is the rapid rise in Canada's civilian labour force. In 1945 the total civilian labour force in Canada was 4,481,000 while today it is 5,230,000, an increase of 749,000 persons. The increase for the past year was 36,000 persons. It might be of some help in

The Budget-Mr. MacEachen putting this problem of unemployment in perspective if we consider the number of employed as well as the number of unemployed. The dominion bureau of statistics figure for persons without jobs and seeking work as of February 1954 was 312,000, which is the highest figure for this category since and including the year 1945. At the same time the total number with jobs in Canada as of February, 1954 was 4,918,000. This figure demonstrates that there were more persons with jobs in Canada in February 1954 than at the same time in 1945, 1946, 1947, 1948, 1949 and 1950. According to the recent D.B.S. labour supplement there are more jobs in Canada now than in 1951 or 1952.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is true that the number of jobs in this country have decreased since last year at the same time by 97,000, and while I lament and I am distressed as much as hon. members opposite at the number of unemployed in the country I still believe that in order to maintain a balance we should also rejoice that the Canadian economy is, as of now, maintaining employment for almost five million Canadians.
Naturally a growing population combined with an expanding economy will result in an expanded labour force, and if our economy, Mr. Speaker, is in for a period of general readjustment then it might be wise for hon. members of this house to consider how the expansion of the labour force could be arrested during this temporary period. One of the most obvious devices that occurs to me is an increased emphasis on vocational education in necessary skills in Canada.
May I turn now to another aspect of the budget. The total non-defence budgetary expenditures in round figures amounted to two and a half billion dollars. Two-thirds of this amount is accounted for by interest and service on the public debt, social security benefits, subsidies and tax rental payments to the provinces, and services and assistance to agriculture.
I should like to discuss two classes of expenditure mentioned by the minister, namely, tax rental payments and social security benefits, with particular reference to my own province of Nova Scotia.
In my judgment the tax rental agreements have served or achieved two ends. First, by agreement with the provinces, they have permitted the federal government to become the chief collector of corporation and income taxes, providing the central government not only with this rich source of revenue but


also giving the central government weapons of the first importance in controlling the economy.
Second, these tax agreements have attempted to overcome disparities in economic development as between parts of Canada by effecting what amounts to a regional redistribution of government revenue. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953, the total revenue collected by the province of Nova Scotia amounted to approximately $48 million. Of that amount approximately $20 million was revenue under the tax rental agreements. Had the province of Nova Scotia cultivated these tax fields on its own its collections would have fallen far short of payments under the tax rental agreements, and that province would have been unable to provide the standard of service now available to the residents of that province. Even with the tax rental agreements, there is considerable strain on the province of Nova Scotia in attempting to meet the standards of the wealthier provinces of Canada. Though the tax rental agreements have been of undoubted value to the province of Nova Scotia, I am sure I will be forgiven by hon. members if I confess that I have always shared the view, so frequently expressed by Premier Macdonald of Nova Scotia, that a more efficacious method of handling the province of Nova Scotia would have been to adopt the principle of fiscal need first recommended by the Rowell-Sirois commission, and later incorporated in the original proposals made to the province.
May I turn now, Mr. Speaker, to a few remarks on the subject of social security and its contribution to the national life. The comprehensive system of social security in Canada is meeting the needs that arise in an acute form in any industrial or market economy. In such an economy, income from gainful employment is the source of livelihood for large classifications of people. The loss of income, through causes beyond the control of the individual, and the inability to accumulate savings to meet the critical emergencies of life have been the principal considerations which have led modern governments to establish programs of social security. I am proud, Mr. Speaker, of Canada's achievement in this field because through this medium we have relieved human insecurity in critical areas of life and we have met the challenge of problems associated with industrialization.
At one period of time the chief support for social security came solely from persons who wished to relieve human suffering, and I trust that such motivation will continue to be the

basic philosophy of our approach to the problem. But to those supporting social security unexpected aid came from economic science. Economic science proved, I think without any doubt, that social security or transfer payments constitute a permanent support to purchasing power and contribute to the desirable social and economic objective of overcoming inequities in the distribution of income.
The work of the government in this direction has not ceased. As a new member of this house, I received my greatest satisfaction from the announcement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) that assistance would be provided for disabled persons. The Nova Scotia legislature aas passed enabling legislation in order to be .n a position to adopt this legislation.
I have mentioned particularly the tax rental agreements and social security payments principally because they indicate the direction of government expenditures. I believe that these two policies have been instruments that have increased the appreciation of Canadian citizenship. There are no other two policies that indicate more clearly the manner in which this government has met the challenge of Canadian federalism. It is true, Mr. Speaker, that in the province of Nova Scotia at present there are difficulties that no one should overlook. There is particularly the difficulty associated with the coal and steel industries. But because an opportunity will foe provided to discuss this matter when the estimates of the dominion coal board come before the house I shall postpone my remarks on these subjects until that time.
Mr. Speaker, if the claim is made that those who strike an optimistic note are wishful thinkers, then I want to join that band of persons who have faith in the future of Canada, that group which is not dismayed by a single temporary interruption in the steady growth of the Canadian economy.

speechtext:
I am having as much difficulty, Mr. Speaker, as I sometimes have when asking a question on the orders of the day.
In his budget speech the other night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) made this statement upon which I wish to comment briefly. As recorded at page 3730 of Hansard for April 6 the minister referred at some length to the matter of the old age security fund, and then said this:
Looking at the year just beginning, it seems probable that we shall again have a deficit of about $50 million. A precise accounting approach might suggest that I ought to propose an increase in the scale of contributions; but, as I said a few minutes ago, I do not think this is a time to be increasing taxes in Canada if that can possibly be avoided. I propose therefore to carry on with the same scale of contributions for another year.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, I do not quarrel with the statement of the minister that he does not propose to make any increases in the taxes provided under the Old Age Security Act, so far as this year is concerned. But I do wish to register my strong objection to the inference that the day might come when, because of deficits being incurred- bookkeeping deficits, if one might call them that-in the old age security fund it might be


necessary to propose an increase in one or other of the 2 per cent taxes levied for purposes of the old age security fund.
The fact that that inference is there is supported by various news reports commenting on what the Minister of Finance said in the paragraph I have just read. For example, under the byline of Warren Baldwin, the Ottawa Citizen of Wednesday, April 7, 1954, had this to say:
Canadian taxpayers have been given another year of grace before being put on a pay-as-you-go basis for payment of old age pensions. They will continue to contribute two per cent in sales tax, two per cent through corporation tax and two per cent on personal incomes up to $60.
Faced with the alternative of increasing his overall tax structure or budgeting for a deficit, Finance Minister Abbott has avoided both and put off the day of reckoning.
Similarly, the Ottawa Citizen in its editorial on the minister's budget, also in the issue of April 7, referred to this act of the minister in these words: "And so he temporizes for another year." The point I wish to make is this, that we are paying for old age pensions now on a pay-as-we-go basis. The fact that the total cost of old age security payments at their present level of $40 a month is not covered by the earmarked taxes does not mean that those payments are not being made out of current income. The fact is that old age security payments at the present time are being made in part from these three 2 per cent taxes, and in part from revenues out of the consolidated revenue fund, but all of these revenues are equally current.
In my view, the point should be made that there is nothing wrong with the payments being met as they are today. In fact
1	go further and say it is better that these payments be met in that way than that the
2	per cent social security tax should be increased in order that there might be a bookkeeping balance. So long as the present situation is maintained, to the extent that old age security payments are met in part out of the consolidated revenue fund, to that extent they are paid for on an ability to pay basis, to an extent that is greater than is the case with respect to the 2-2-2 formula. The funds that are received into the consolidated revenue fund on the basis of the personal income tax and on the basis of the corporation income tax are on a much more progressive basis than is the case with the three 2 per cent taxes. I want to register my very strong protest at any

suggestion that there should be any increase next year or the year after in those 2 per cent taxes that are collected for the purpose of old age security.
In fact, as hon. members know, when these three 2 per cent taxes were brought in we objected to certain features of them. For example, we objected to the fact that the tax on personal incomes for purposes of the old age security fund was not put on a graduated basis. In addition to it not being on a graduated basis, it is cut off at the $60 point, and we objected very strongly to that. We agree that old age security pensions should be on a contributory basis and they are; yes, they should be on a pay-as-you-go basis, and they are; but we also contend that they should be on an ability to pay basis. That is not the case if you insist on balancing the old age security fund by 2-2-2 tax, or a 3-3-3 or a 4-4-4 formula, or whatever the minister may devise.
To the extent that old age security payments are paid out of the general revenues, out of revenues collected from the income tax and the corporation tax, to that extent they are being paid on a fairer basis than is the case with respect to the formula set up in the Old Age Security Act. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I meant what I said when I started this speech, in spite of the fact the minister and other members were surprised and gave me that questionable applause. I meant to speak only for these few minutes to underline the point that there should not be any increase this year, next year or in future years in these special taxes under which old age security payments are made at the present time.
If additional moneys are needed, let them be found by increasing the income tax in the upper brackets, let them be found by increasing the corporation tax. While I am referring to this matter, Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that the time has come-my leader suggested it this afternoon in his remarks- for an increase in the old age pension itself. My leader pointed out that the federal government as long ago as 1945 had described itself as ready to accept the full responsibility for adequate old age pensions for all our people 70 years of age and over and of participating in adequate pensions from 65 to 69. The sum of $40 a month is not an adequate pension at the present time. I suggest that at the very least that figure 83276-254
The Budget-Mr. Knowles should be $60 a month, and that could be paid and should be paid at the present time.
I strongly urge, Mr. Speaker, the view of the man in the street that it is very strange that parliament can find so much money for so many other purposes but cannot find it for increasing old age pensions. To the ordinary Canadian this is a sad commentary on the way in which this government operates. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, far from putting any pressure on the country to get ready for the idea of an increase in the old age security tax, I say that this tax should stay where it is or be reduced, but that the old age pension should be increased and that the funds necessary for increasing the amount of the old age pension should come out of general revenues on the basis of the income tax structure and on the basis of the corporation tax, for those are taxes which are paid according to ability to pay.
Just in the two or three minutes that remain to ten o'clock-and I am not adjourning the debate, Mr. Speaker, for as I said when I started, I wanted to speak just very briefly on this question-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the two or three minutes that are left I wish to say that in addition to my feeling that something should be done at this session of parliament to raise the old age pension, I certainly hope that if nothing is placed on the order paper of this House of Commons before we go home for Easter, when we come back we shall find on the order paper notice of legislation to increase the amount of the war veterans allowance. I was hoping today that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in reply to my question on the orders of the day would be able to tell us before we go home for Easter what legislation remains to be introduced during the balance of the session, and that his answer would have included an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act. I urge, sir, very strongly that along with an increase in the old age pension, the old age assistance pension-and the blind pension too-there should be an increase in the war veterans allowance and in the permissible income allowed to recipients of that pension.
If anyone is saying: Oh, there is the C.C.F. again, asking for payments, asking for increases in old age pensions but not proposing any means for raising the money, I suggest,

The Budget-Mr. Knowles Mr. Speaker, that there is on the order paper in my name a motion which I cannot now debate because of the rules of the house, asking for an elimination of the $60 ceiling on the old age security tax, for this very purpose; and just a few moments ago there was before this house an amendment in the name of my leader asking for an increase in income taxes in the upper brackets and for an increase in corporation taxes. When we make such proposals we have it in mind that that is a way in which money can be found to increase old age pensions and make these

other improvements in social legislation which we feel should be made at this session of parliament.
On motion of Mr. Drew the debate was adjourned.
